articles.title: US Pushes Stronger ASEAN Naval Cooperation as South China Sea Disputes Raise Regional Security Concerns - Wake Up Singapore
articles.summary: US Pushes Stronger ASEAN Naval Cooperation as South China Sea Disputes Raise Regional Security Concerns  Wake Up Singapore
articles.full_text:
Philippines: The United States is seeking closer military cooperation with Southeast Asian countries, with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth proposing a new defence framework and stronger joint naval operations amid continuing tensions in the South China Sea.
Hegseth made the proposal during the ASEAN-US Defence Ministers’ Informal Meeting in Cebu on Wednesday, where he called for greater coordination between regional armed forces.
Footage shows Philippine Defence Secretary Gilbert Teodoro welcoming Hegseth before the two officials joined other ASEAN defence ministers for discussions and group photographs.
Washington’s proposed plans include improving maritime surveillance, expanding joint military exercises and strengthening cooperation between regional navies.
“Serious partners train together, learn together, plan together, and build the confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict,” Hegseth said.
He also reaffirmed Washington’s commitment to working with Southeast Asian countries to maintain regional stability.
“The United States is a proud Pacific nation, and alongside our ASEAN partners, we are resolved to deliver peace through strength, peace, prosperity and sovereignty for all member nations based on mutual respect,” he added.
US Proposes New Defence Framework
One of the key proposals discussed was a new US-ASEAN defence cooperation framework designed to guide military collaboration over the coming years.
The initiative comes as Southeast Asian nations prepare for further regional defence discussions, with Singapore scheduled to chair the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) in 2027.
The proposed framework could provide a platform for expanding cooperation in maritime security, military training and coordination between armed forces.
Hegseth also highlighted the importance of building stronger relationships between Washington and its Southeast Asian partners as regional security challenges continue.
Philippines Backs Stronger US Military Presence
Philippine Defence Secretary Gilbert Teodoro welcomed Washington’s continued involvement in Southeast Asian security, describing a strong US presence as important for regional peace and stability.
He also stressed the importance of maintaining freedom of navigation, particularly for countries that depend on international maritime routes for trade and economic activity.
“The Philippines hopes to build on these efforts in the years to come. Because all of us have relied and will continue to rely on freedom of navigation for the security, prosperity and resilience of our people,” Teodoro said.
The meeting also coincided with the 80th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the Philippines and the United States.
Hegseth further pointed to the 50th anniversary of formal US-ASEAN relations in 2027, describing it as another opportunity to strengthen military partnerships.
South China Sea Remains A Major Concern
The discussions come amid repeated confrontations in the disputed South China Sea, where several countries have overlapping territorial claims.
China claims large areas of the waterway, while the Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia also maintain claims over parts of the region.
The Philippines and China have repeatedly clashed over access to contested waters, making maritime security a major concern for governments across Southeast Asia.
The latest US proposal highlights Washington’s efforts to expand its defence partnerships in the region as disputes over navigation and territorial claims continue.
With Singapore preparing to chair the ADMM in 2027, regional defence cooperation is expected to remain an important topic for ASEAN members and their international partners.

articles.title: Why Southeast Asia has attracted strong FDI inflows, from advanced manufacturing to the digital economy - Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.summary: Why Southeast Asia has attracted strong FDI inflows, from advanced manufacturing to the digital economy  Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.full_text:
Uncertainty has become the new normal for global businesses, with a mix of geopolitical tensions and macroeconomic concerns forcing them to prioritise resilience and restructure supply chains. This has impacted global Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), which fell by 11 per cent in 2024, following a 10 per cent drop in 2023, according to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025.
Against this backdrop, Southeast Asia has defied the odds and emerged as the bright spot for growth, with foreign direct investment (FDI) growing year on year. In 2024, Southeast Asia accounted for 15 per cent of global FDI inflows, attracting US$226 billion, a rise of 8 per cent from 2023. Since 2021, annual FDI inflows have consistently exceeded US$200 billion, above the previous decade’s annual average of under US$130 billion.
In fact, FDI stock in ASEAN rose from US$1 trillion in 2010 to US$3.6 trillion in 2024, equivalent to 1.2 times the combined stock in Africa and South America. Here are five highlights from the report that explain why MNCs are doubling down on Southeast Asia and why Singapore is their strategic hub for expansion.
1. More greenfield investments across diverse manufacturing sectors
Investments into Southeast Asia are increasingly driven by new and expansionary projects. More than two-thirds of inflows comprise of equity capital, while cross-border mergers and acquisitions fell by 61 per cent from 2023.
This signals that businesses are not simply acquiring firms or restructuring their balance sheets. Instead, they are establishing new operations, expanding production capacity, and building long-term capabilities across the region.
Furthermore, manufacturing FDI rose sharply, increasing by 147 per cent year-on-year, particularly in supply chain-intensive sectors such as automotive, electronics and semiconductors. Many of these big-ticket investments were either first-time entries into Southeast Asia or involved significant upgrading and expansion of existing facilities. These investments were driven by rising regional demand and the adoption of advanced manufacturing technologies to improve efficiency and resilience.
Investment spanned major economies, with Chinese firms active in automotive and apparel, US firms in pharmaceuticals and semiconductors, UK investors in aerospace and energy, and other Asian multinationals across automotive and electronics.
2. Digital economy investment is accelerating
Alongside manufacturing growth, investment in Southeast Asia’s digital economy is rising rapidly. Greenfield investment in digital-related sectors more than doubled to US$16 billion in 2024, reflecting rising demand and growing investor confidence in the region’s digital infrastructure, connectivity, and technology ecosystem.
This growth was driven by expansion in data centres, cloud services, software development and technology-enabled business activities. These investments are critical as they strengthen the region’s digital backbone – supporting advanced manufacturing, supply chain coordination, digital trade and cross-border services.
Some of these investments in Singapore include Amazon’s AWS APAC Hub, OpenAI’s APAC Hub, and Databrick’s Asia Pacific & Japan Hub.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a key digital technology across Southeast Asia, with companies adopting AI to enhance their supply chains by optimising logistics and improving inventory management. Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand are leading the region in industrial robot installations, with Singapore ranking second globally in robot density, with 730 robots per 10,000 employees in 2023 – significantly above the global average of 162.

articles.title: The 20-Year Leap: How Vietnam’s Factory-First Engine Left Indonesia Behind - InvestorTrust
articles.summary: The 20-Year Leap: How Vietnam’s Factory-First Engine Left Indonesia Behind  InvestorTrust
articles.full_text:
The 20-Year Leap: How Vietnam’s Factory-First Engine Left Indonesia Behind
Key Takeaways
| ● | Vietnam's nominal GDP per capita is projected to reach $5,259 this year, officially surpassing Indonesia's $5,153 according to latest International Monetary Fund estimates. | 
| ● | The economic inflection caps a structural divergence two decades in the making, heralded in 2005 when Vietnam's per capita electricity generation first crossed above Indonesia's. | 
| ● | High-tech manufacturing drives nearly 25% of Vietnam's economy compared to roughly 19% in Indonesia, cementing Hanoi as a premier global hub for electronics and semiconductors. | 
| ● | Indonesian business lobby Kadin has outlined an aggressive "5D" strategy and eight industry task forces to accelerate domestic competitiveness and escape the middle-income trap. | 
A multi-level highway interchange illuminates evening traffic in Ho Chi Minh City as industrial infrastructure outlays accelerate across Vietnam. Photo: VnExpress
JAKARTA, Investortrust.id — A historic economic milestone is unfolding across Southeast Asia. According to the International Monetary Fund’s October World Economic Outlook, Vietnam’s gross domestic product per capita is projected to reach $5,259 this year, eclipsing Indonesia’s $5,153. The figures represent an 8.9% year-on-year advance for Hanoi, almost doubling its nominal output per person over the past decade, while pushing Vietnam into fifth place among ASEAN members behind Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia, and Thailand.
The IMF projects Vietnam will maintain its per-capita lead into 2027, reaching $5,659 against Indonesia’s $5,550. While Indonesia remains the undisputed heavyweight of Southeast Asia in absolute terms—commanding a $1.48 trillion overall GDP against Vietnam’s $542 billion due to a population nearly three times larger—the per-person inversion marks a watershed realignment for the region’s balance of economic momentum.
Per capita income is the ultimate barometer of national productivity and living standards. For decades, Indonesia stood comfortably ahead of Vietnam, holding an estimated $250 lead as recently as last year. That Vietnam has leapfrogged the archipelago underscores how relentlessly focused industrial policy, trade openness, and aggressive capital deepening can outflank a resource-rich domestic consumption giant. As multilateral institutions forecast Vietnam's economy to expand 8.4% this year alongside a blazing 9.95% third-quarter print, Indonesia's steady 5% trajectory is proving insufficient to defend its regional hierarchy.
A Divergence Twenty Years in the Making
While headline observers treat the 2026 per-capita flip as a sudden development, the underlying shift has been two decades in the making.
Data on industrial energy consumption shows that Vietnam’s annual per capita electricity generation first crossed above Indonesia’s back in 2005. That subtle inflection signaled that Vietnam had begun electrifying and equipping its workforce at a far more aggressive velocity. Over the subsequent twenty years, Vietnam’s power buildout climbed almost vertically, surging from parity to over 3,000 kilowatt-hours per person by 2024, more than double Indonesia's generation rate.
Because electricity consumption in developing economies tracks factory tooling, automated assembly lines, and industrial capacity, Vietnam’s surging grid was the advance indicator of its factory-first transformation. While Indonesia’s per capita power growth climbed at an incremental incline, Vietnam was building the generation capacity necessary to power continuous shifts of high-tech production.
Factory Floor vs. Commodity Vault
The root of Hanoi's per-capita ascent lies in the sheer manufacturing intensity of its economy. Manufacturing value-added accounts for roughly 25% of Vietnam's GDP, acting as the primary engine of national expansion. When including the broader industry and construction envelope, that footprint accounts for nearly 37% to 44% of total output.
By comparison, manufacturing’s contribution to Indonesia's gross domestic product has dwindled from approximately 32% in 2002 to roughly 19% today. Instead of scaling high-tech factory floors, Indonesia rode successive commodity booms across coal and palm oil, leaving its economy anchored by extractive primary sectors and low-productivity informal services.
Vietnam capitalized on global supply chain realignments, embedding itself directly into Tier-1 multinational production networks. Global titans such as Taiwan’s Foxconn and South Korea’s Samsung Electronics turned northern Vietnam into a dominant production base for smartphones, semiconductors, and precision components. Supported by an expansive public investment push totaling VND 1.014 quadrillion ($39.3 billion) this year for highways, ports, and airports, Vietnam is targeting full-year growth of at least 10% on its way toward an $8,500 per capita milestone by 2030.
Indonesia Counters With Reindustrialization Drive
Despite Vietnam's milestone, Indonesian business leaders and policymakers insist that the nation's economic potential remains unmatched if it can successfully execute structural reindustrialization.
Addressing delegates at the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kadin) National Leadership Meeting (Rapimnas) in Jakarta on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, Kadin Chairman Anindya Novyan Bakrie emphasized that the business community is actively building economic shock absorbers while mounting a nationwide competitiveness campaign.
"We do not see this as a crisis, but it is a formidable challenge," Bakrie told reporters, noting that corporate balance sheets and household purchasing power must be protected through close coordination between the private sector and the central government.
Bakrie underscored that 92% of Indonesia's gross domestic product is generated outside the central government budget, making private enterprise and industrial execution the definitive arbiters of long-term wealth. To reclaim momentum, Kadin is spearheading an operational "5D" strategy centered on fiscal discipline and decentralization, aggressive deregulation, operational debottlenecking, sovereign capital deployment through investment agency Danantara, and systematic capacity upgrades for micro, small, and medium enterprises.
To prevent plans from stalling in rhetoric, Kadin has established eight specialized task forces evaluated on rolling quarterly performance cycles, targeting supply-chain integration, mineral downstreaming, human capital productivity, and energy sovereignty. Bakrie introduced the twin national rallying cries of "Buy Indonesia" to draw patient direct investment into physical capacity, and "Buy from Indonesia" to integrate domestic producers into 77 premier global supplier networks spanning aerospace to electric transport.
Bakrie concluded that the ultimate goal is converting Indonesia's historic crisis endurance into proactive global competitiveness, presenting the chamber's roadmap directly to President Prabowo Subianto.
"Indonesia’s resilience has been tested and proven across generations," Bakrie said. "What we must now step forward and deliver is our competitiveness."

articles.title: Vietnam and ASEAN move to elevate position in global value chain - Vietnam Economic Times
articles.summary: Vietnam and ASEAN move to elevate position in global value chain  Vietnam Economic Times
articles.full_text:
During the discussion session “Repositioning Vietnam - ASEAN in Global Value Chains” on October 27, co-organized by the World Economic Forum (WEF) and the Fourth Industrial Revolution Center in Vietnam (C4IR), in the framework of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026 in Ho Chị Minh City, representatives from businesses, international organizations, and regulatory agencies pointed out that attracting investment in the ASEAN region is just the beginning.
The greater challenge is how domestic enterprises can participate more deeply in the regional production network, enhance added value, and better utilize the capital and technology flows moving into ASEAN.
ASEAN attracts investors but internal connectivity remains limited
According to Mr. Kyriakos Triantafyllidis, Head of Growth and Strategy, Centre for Advanced Manufacturing and Supply Chains, under the World Economic Forum (WEF), ASEAN currently has about 700 million people, with a combined economic scale of $4.3 trillion. By 2025, the region was expected to attract $245 billion in FDI, a 10 percent increase from the previous year.
The proportion of foreign-origin value in Vietnam's exports increased from about 33 percent in 2010 to nearly 50 percent in 2022. This indicates that Vietnam's exports are increasingly dependent on imported materials, components, and inputs.
To create more value domestically, Vietnam needs to enhance the capacity of local enterprises to participate more deeply in supply chains and become tier-1 suppliers for FDI corporations. On a regional scale, intra-ASEAN trade accounts for only about one-fifth of the region's total trade turnover, indicating that member economies still have significant room to strengthen connectivity and production cooperation.
These issues require ASEAN not only to continue attracting investment and expanding exports but also to develop the capacity of local enterprises, strengthen supply chain links within the region, and participate more deeply in high-value stages such as technology, design, and product innovation.
Expert perspectives on trade and investment potential
Mr. Sacha Dray, an Economist at the World Bank in Economic Policy Unit for Vietnam, agreed that ASEAN has a favorable foundation for trade and investment development, with abundant labor, high trade openness, and an extensive network of trade agreements. However, the region has not yet fully exploited the benefits of integration.
In terms of production, ASEAN has deeply participated in the global value chain, from automobile and electric vehicle production in Thailand, assembly in Vietnam, to semiconductor manufacturing, testing, and packaging in Malaysia and Singapore. However, the intra-regional value chain remains limited: global value chain participation based on regional links accounts for only about one-third in ASEAN, compared to 70 percent in the EU.
Specifically, of ASEAN’s total export turnover of about $2 trillion, only 22 percent is consumed within the region, compared to about 60 percent in the EU. This makes ASEAN economies more dependent on external demand, while also limiting the ability to spread benefits among countries in the region.
According to Mr. Dre, the income disparity among member countries - where the gap between the poorest and richest nation reaches up to 70 times, compared to eight times in the EU- also creates uneven market demand and resource allocation. To bridge this gap, he suggested increasing cross-border investment among ASEAN countries, connecting foreign enterprises with local suppliers, and removing non-tariff barriers.
Business views on ASEAN’s appeal
From a business perspective, Ms. Jessica Nguyen, General Director, Country Holding Officer, and Board Chairwoman of ABB Vietnam, believes that ASEAN’s appeal comes from three factors: market size; increasingly developed production capacity; and regional connectivity.
According to her, ASEAN no longer competes solely on low labor costs. Evidence is that Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia are investing more in advanced manufacturing, digitization, and developing technical human resources. At the same time, trade agreements and regional connectivity allow businesses to build supply chains across multiple countries instead of being limited to a single market.
Trust in the supply chain is built through quality, traceability, reliability, and product consistency. These are the conditions for Vietnamese suppliers to transition from fulfilling orders to becoming partners with higher technical and management capabilities.
However, after more than 32 years of operation in Vietnam, ABB observed that technology and machinery can be acquired relatively quickly, whereas operational and management capabilities take time to build. “The long-term value that multinational corporations bring is not just automation equipment, but also operational knowledge, global standards, and the ability to build resilient supply chains,” Ms. Nguyen emphasized.
Policy recommendations for supplier development
From a state management perspective, Ms. Pham Quynh Mai, Deputy Director General of the Multilateral Trade Policy Department under the Ministry of Industry and Trade, noted that reducing tariffs is not enough to promote regional trade. ASEAN countries need to address behind-the-border barriers, including customs procedures, standards, certifications, logistics, and differences in rules of origin among trade agreements.
According to her, the time and costs incurred at each stage, from sourcing materials, organizing production, meeting rules of origin to transportation and delivery, all affect the efficiency of the entire supply chain. Therefore, ASEAN needs to enhance information exchange, improve enforcement capacity, and limit the duplication of inspection and certification procedures.
For Vietnam, she proposed building a national supplier development program involving the Ministry of Industry and Trade, local governments, industry associations, and FDI enterprises. This program would help small and medium-sized enterprises access finance for technology investment, production upgrades, and workforce training.
The Autumn Economic Forum 2026, themed “The Convergence of New Global Growth Poles,” took place from October 26 to October 29 in Ho Chi Minh City, directed by Prime Minister Le Minh Hung and chaired by the Ho Chi Minh City People’s Committee in collaboration with C4IR.

articles.title: ASEAN Parliamentarians denounce Myanmar’s cyber-security law - Assam Times
articles.summary: ASEAN Parliamentarians denounce Myanmar’s cyber-security law  Assam Times
articles.full_text:
Guwahati: The ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR) opposes the military junta’s recently revived cyber-security law with a warning that it would pose a serious threat to fundamental rights and contradicts the principles enlisted in the Constitution of Myanmar. The draconian legislation is a calculated attempt by the junta to suppress dissents, stifle free expressions and violate the privacy of Myanmarese nationals, added the APHR, a regional network of current and former Parliamentarians belonging to southeast Asian nations.
Expected to come into force next week, the law grants the military sweeping and unchecked powers under the pretext of national security. These powers enable the regime to censor public discourse, dominate digital platforms and restrict access to independent information. By institutionalizing mass surveillance, the law severely undermines privacy and individual freedoms, obstructing the efforts of pro-democracy advocates and civil society organizations striving for justice and accountability in the country, said an APHR statement issued from Jakarta on 24 January 2025.
“The true purpose of this law is to eliminate any opposition to the regime and solidify its grip on power,” said Mercy Chriesty Barends, APHR co-chairperson and a lawmaker in Indonesia’s House of Representatives. It flagrantly contradicts Myanmar’s own constitution, which guarantees the rights to free expression and privacy. As parliamentarians committed to defending human rights, we stand unequivocally with the people of Myanmar and the activists, journalists, and civil society groups who are directly threatened by this oppressive measure, she added.
One of the law’s most chilling provisions criminalizes the use of virtual private networks (VPNs), essential tools for bypassing censorship and accessing independent information. This alarming move exemplifies the junta’s efforts to monitor, censor and control online activities, creating a climate of fear and constant surveillance.
“This law’s demand for forced data handovers and invasive monitoring highlights the regime’s blatant disregard for both human rights and constitutional guidelines,” said Charles Santiago, APHR co-chairperson and a former lawmaker of  Malaysian Parliament. Not only does it violate the fundamental freedoms of Myanmar’s citizens, but also undermines the rule of law by enacting measures that contradict the constitution’s protection of individual rights. This is nothing short of a formalisation of the junta’s escalating abuses, added the former lawmaker.
“This proposed cyber-security law must be withdrawn immediately,” asserted Arlene D Brosas, an APHR board member and lawmaker in the Philippines House of Representatives. She furthermore shared that it was shelved in previous years due to overwhelming national and international oppositions and the current draft is no better. It demands urgent resistance from both the region and the global community.
If enacted, the proposed law will deal a death blow to Myanmar’s online civic space. It threatens to obliterate freedom of expression, association and access to information. Its provisions are intentionally crafted to dominate every aspect of the digital sphere, escalating surveillance, censoring dissent and stifling any form of political opposition. This blatant attempt to crush Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement demands a resolute and unified response from the global community.
The forum of Parliamentarians now calls on the international community to take immediate action by denouncing this law and exerting diplomatic pressure on Myanmar’s military junta to abandon it. Governments, media outlets and human rights organisations must unite to denounce this oppressive legislation, which directly undermines the right of Myanmarese to express themselves freely in a safe and open digital environment.
“This draconian law must be repealed urgently,” stated Rangsiman Rome, an APHR board member and lawmaker in the Thai Parliament. The people of Myanmar deserve a future where their rights are protected, their voices are heard, and their freedoms are preserved. Otherwise, this law will only further tighten the junta’s grip on power, suffocating freedoms and entrenching their illegitimate control over the country, he concluded.

articles.title: Guest Column | ASEAN Breaks the Ice With Myanmar, But Skepticism Runs Deep - The Irrawaddy
articles.summary: Guest Column | ASEAN Breaks the Ice With Myanmar, But Skepticism Runs Deep  The Irrawaddy
articles.full_text:
BANGKOK—For the first time since the 2021 coup upended Myanmar’s place in the region, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s foreign ministers sat down face to face with their Myanmar counterpart on Sunday. The meeting, hosted by Thailand in Bangkok, was billed by its architects as a modest but meaningful step forward. Journalists in the room were far less convinced.
Within minutes of the two chief negotiators— Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, ASEAN’s special envoy on Myanmar, and Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow—taking their seats, the press conference turned pointed.
Reporters pressed the pair on whether ASEAN was clinging to a five-point peace plan that Myanmar’s own parliamentarians have publicly dismissed as irrelevant, whether inviting Myanmar’s junta-appointed foreign minister back to the table set a dangerous precedent, and whether any of the “concrete and demonstrable progress” ASEAN says it wants will ever be measured against an actual timeline.
None of those questions received a firm answer. That gap—between ASEAN’s language of cautious optimism and its inability to say when, or how, progress will be judged—is likely to define how this latest overture to Myanmar is read across the region.
A first meeting, five years in the making
Sunday’s engagement was, in diplomatic terms, unusually layered. It comprised two distinct sessions: an informal meeting of ASEAN foreign ministers including Myanmar’s foreign minister, U Tin Maung Swe, and a separate Extended Informal Consultation on Myanmar involving the other ASEAN members.
Ten of the bloc’s 11 members attended in Bangkok, all at the foreign minister level, barring Malaysia, which sent its secretary-general for senior officials. Cambodia was the sole no-show, declining to send any representative.
Lazaro, who has held the special envoy brief since the Philippines took over as ASEAN chair, called the session historic in scale, if not in substance.
“This is the first time that we have met in person with the foreign minister of Myanmar since the events in 2021,” she told reporters, describing a “comprehensive briefing” from Myanmar’s side covering the peace process, the transfer of Daw Aung San Suu Kyi to a designated residence, and cooperation against cross-border scam operations, trafficking and drug trafficking.
Sihasak, whose government brokered the encounter, was careful to frame it as an evolution in tactics rather than a change in position.
“Thailand supports the approach of calibrated engagement,” he said. “All of us reaffirm our commitment to the Five-Point Consensus [5PC], but the key issue here is what is the strategy to implement it.”
He added a pointed caveat aimed at Naypyitaw as much as at ASEAN’s own capitals: “This calibrated engagement is a two-way street… the Myanmar side has to reach out as well to address the concerns of ASEAN and the concerns of the international community.”
The concrete deliverable: a humanitarian mission
If the meeting produced one tangible outcome, it was Lazaro’s announcement that she intends to travel to Myanmar on a humanitarian mission in the second half of this year, working alongside the AHA Center, humanitarian actors and ASEAN development partners to expand access to affected communities.
Both she and Sihasak presented this as evidence that engagement, however slow, is yielding movement.
“This is already a movement,” Lazaro said of Myanmar’s apparent openness to granting permits for humanitarian access to previously restricted areas. “It can’t be done in one stroke.”
Beyond the humanitarian mission, ASEAN’s requests remained the same four benchmarks reiterated throughout the press conference: expanded humanitarian access, a further reduction in violence against civilians, inclusive political dialogue involving all stakeholders, and a more conducive political environment, including further release of political prisoners.
Sihasak said Thailand was also working to facilitate dialogue between Naypyitaw and ethnic armed groups along the Thai border, though he offered no further detail beyond confirming talks were “in the works”.
Old doubts persist beneath the diplomacy
The skepticism voiced by journalists tracked three separate fault lines, and neither official fully dispelled them.
The first concerned the 5PC itself. Asked how ASEAN could keep citing a framework that Myanmar’s own parliament has rejected as “no longer relevant”, Lazaro did not dispute the rejection but held the line regardless: “Whether they reject it or not, I stand [firm], and I think ASEAN stands behind the Five-Point Consensus.”
Sihasak’s answer leaned instead on strategy over principle, arguing Thailand was less interested in “just repeating” the consensus than in working out how to implement it.
The second concerned precedent: whether allowing Myanmar’s foreign minister back into the room—after Naypyitaw had rebuffed ASEAN’s request to allow the special envoy to meet Daw Aung San Suu Kyi directly—rewarded non-compliance.
Lazaro rejected the framing outright, calling the meeting itself the sign of movement, not a concession: “This is the first time we’re meeting… since 2021 when this started in Brunei.”
The third, and perhaps sharpest, concerned accountability: with no dates attached to any of the benchmarks ASEAN has set, how will anyone know whether Myanmar has actually delivered? Here both officials essentially conceded the point.
“It’s evolving. We cannot set dates,” Lazaro admitted, adding that “sometimes the process is more important than… the conclusion.”
Sihasak pointed to this year’s ASEAN Summit as the de facto checkpoint: “We will review and look at whether there’s been substantial progress,” he said, but stopped short of describing any formal mechanism for that review.
Daw Aung San Suu Kyi and the legitimacy question
Questions about Daw Aung San Suu Kyi’s welfare and the legitimacy of Myanmar’s recent election drew some of the meeting’s more delicate exchanges.
Lazaro relayed Myanmar’s assurance that the Nobel laureate remains “in good health” and that the regime would “take care of her”, but acknowledged ASEAN had pressed, without success so far, for the special envoy to be allowed to verify this in person.
On the election that installed Myanmar’s current government, Lazaro was candid about a split within the bloc.
“There are certain countries who have already expressed a possible recalibration of their relations with Myanmar as a result of the recent elections,” she said, while noting that “some ASEAN member states” still consider the vote’s legitimacy unresolved, tying the disagreement back once more to unmet Five-Point Consensus benchmarks.
What comes next
For all the caveats, both officials sought to end the session on a note of open-endedness rather than failure.
“We are ready to help,” Sihasak said. “We are ready to assist in order that we would like Myanmar not to be [absent] from the ASEAN family.”
Lazaro echoed the sentiment, calling the day’s talks “an impetus for further engagement” toward a solution she stressed must ultimately be “Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led”.
Whether Sunday’s meeting marks the start of a genuine thaw or simply resets the clock on a five-year stalemate is likely to be tested well before the year is out.
Myanmar’s foreign minister is expected to feature in discussions at the upcoming ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting and Post-Ministerial Conferences, due within days, and ASEAN leaders have effectively penciled in this year’s summit as the moment to judge whether Naypyitaw has moved beyond gestures and into the “concrete and demonstrable progress” that both Lazaro and Sihasak say they are still waiting to see.
Nongluck Ajanapanya is a senior economic journalist covering the macroeconomics, real estate and corporate investment strategies driving growth across Thailand and Southeast Asia.

Total import and export turnover for the first 10 months of 2026 is estimated at 1,010.6 billion USD. The Ministry of Industry and Trade aims for high growth, market diversification, and increased technological content.
According to data from the Import-Export Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), Vietnam's total import and export turnover in the first 10 months of 2026 is estimated to reach US$1,010.6 billion, surpassing the US$1,000 billion mark. In October 2026 alone, this figure reached approximately US$122.2 billion, an increase of 47.6% compared to the same period in 2025.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
In the first 10 months, export turnover is estimated at 499 billion USD, an increase of 27.4% compared to the same period last year. Growth was recorded in both the domestic and foreign direct investment (FDI) sectors. Processed industrial goods continued to play a leading role, accounting for 87.4% of total export turnover.
Many major markets such as China, the United States , the European Union (EU), South Korea, and ASEAN recorded positive export growth.
The trade balance for October 2026 is estimated to have a surplus of $6.8 billion, marking the second consecutive month of surplus. However, for the first 10 months of the year, Vietnam still has a trade deficit of approximately $12.7 billion.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Growth orientation for import and export until 2045
In order to maintain growth momentum and improve the quality of trade activities, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is developing a draft Strategy for Import and Export of Goods until 2030, with a vision to 2045. The strategy aims for high growth, in-depth development, and market diversification.
According to the draft, during the period 2026-2030, goods exports are expected to increase by an average of 15-16% per year, and imports by 12-13% per year, contributing to the achievement of double-digit economic growth targets. By 2045, Vietnam aims to be among the top 10 countries with the largest export turnover and among the top 10 countries with the largest import turnover in the world .
You may also like
The draft also aims to maintain a sustainable merchandise trade surplus. The average trade surplus ratio to total export turnover is projected to reach 3-6% during the period 2026-2030, increasing to 7-10% by 2045.
Besides expanding in scale, import and export activities are oriented towards increasing the processing content and application of science and technology . The export share of the domestic enterprise sector is expected to reach 28-30% of total export turnover by 2030 and 38-40% by 2045.
The target for the proportion of processed or refined goods in total export turnover is 89-90% by 2030 and over 92% by 2045. The target for the proportion of high-tech product exports in the total value of processed and manufactured goods exports is approximately 50% by 2030 and over 55% by 2045.
Market diversification increases adaptability.
Reducing the concentration on a few markets is also a key direction in the draft strategy. By 2030, no export market should account for more than 25% of total export turnover, and no import market should account for more than 35% of total import turnover.
The combined export share to the three largest markets or regions is projected to fall below 55% by 2030 and below 50% by 2045. The number of export markets with a turnover exceeding $1 billion is targeted to surpass 45 by 2030 and reach 55 by 2045.
At the same time, Vietnam aims to increase the proportion of exports to new markets, including South Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Latin America, to approximately 10% by 2030 and 15% by 2045.
Focus on supporting businesses in Q4/2026

In the fourth quarter of 2026, the Ministry of Industry and Trade identified key tasks including boosting exports, diversifying markets, and improving the compliance capacity of businesses. One of the solutions emphasized is effectively utilizing signed free trade agreements (FTAs) while expanding into new markets.
The Ministry also focuses on enhancing early warning capabilities regarding trade defense cases, tariff barriers, green standards, traceability, and rules of origin. Alongside this, it supports businesses in improving product quality, building brands, and ensuring transparency in the supply chain.
Other tasks include promoting official exports, expanding agreements and protocols on agricultural quarantine, increasing investment in cold chain logistics infrastructure, and standardizing growing areas and packaging facilities to meet the regulations of each partner market.

articles.title: Vietnam's import and export trade has reached the $1 trillion mark, affirming its position in global trade. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam's import and export trade has reached the $1 trillion mark, affirming its position in global trade.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Continuously setting new milestones
 In 2026, geopolitical conflicts and ongoing military operations around the world will continue to profoundly impact the structure and pace of global trade. Rising energy prices will drive up production costs, putting inflationary pressure on many major economies. In this context, Vietnam, with its high degree of economic openness, will be directly affected by fluctuations in international trade.
 Despite facing numerous challenges, by October 29, 2026, the total value of Vietnam's goods exports and imports reached a historic milestone of US$1 trillion, with more than two months remaining in the year. Exports totaled approximately US$493.64 billion, an increase of US$105.56 billion, or 27.2%, compared to the same period last year; imports totaled US$507.66 billion, an increase of US$138.72 billion, or 37.6%.
 It is projected that for the whole year of 2026, the value of goods exports will increase by over 25%, exceeding the 15-16% target set by the Government in Appendix IV of Resolution No. 01/NQ-CP. 
|  | 
| Customs officers' operational activities. Photo: Van Ta. | 
 Since joining the World Trade Organization (WTO), Vietnam's import and export activities have continuously set new milestones: US$100 billion in 2007; US$200 billion in 2011; US$300 billion in 2015; US$400 billion in 2017; US$500 billion in 2019; US$600 billion in 2021; US$700 billion in 2022; US$900 billion in 2025 and US$1,000 billion in 2026.
 During the period 2016-2025, the total value of exports and imports reached US$6,120 billion, averaging US$612 billion per year. While this figure was US$351.38 billion in 2016, it increased to US$929.92 billion by 2025, a 2.65-fold increase, equivalent to a US$578.54 billion increase. The average annual growth rate of exports and imports during this period is 11%.
 Currently, Vietnam ranks 18th in the world for exports and 20th for imports. Within the ASEAN region, Vietnam maintains its second position, after Singapore . These results further strengthen Vietnam's role as an important link in the global supply chain.
 Proactively establishing partnerships with other countries, promoting negotiations, signing, and implementing trade agreements has created momentum for exports, contributing to the diversification of markets and products. In particular, Vietnamese agricultural products, seafood, and other products with competitive advantages continue to have more opportunities to access international markets.
 As of October 29, 2026, Vietnam had trade relations with 237 countries and territories; of which, 36 export markets and 31 import markets had a scale exceeding 1 billion USD. Along with efforts to expand markets, ministries, sectors, and localities are stepping up the review and amendment of mechanisms and policies, reducing administrative procedures and costs for businesses.
 In the customs sector, the Ministry of Finance is directing the implementation of comprehensive reforms, from streamlining the organizational structure and improving mechanisms and policies to strengthening risk management and digitizing business processes to provide services anytime, anywhere, and on any device. The synchronized deployment of information technology systems contributes to simplifying procedures, reducing compliance costs, and enhancing transparency in trade activities.
 Along with trade facilitation, efforts to combat smuggling, trade fraud, origin fraud, and intellectual property infringement have been strengthened, contributing to the protection of legitimate businesses and the reputation of Vietnamese goods in the international market.
 FDI enterprises make a significant contribution.
 From the beginning of the year until October 29, 2026, the foreign direct investment (FDI) sector achieved a total import and export value of US$778 billion, accounting for 77.5% of the country's total trade turnover, an increase of 37% compared to the same period last year. Meanwhile, the import and export value of domestic enterprises reached approximately US$223 billion, an increase of 16%.
 Exports to many markets with free trade agreements (FTAs) continued to grow positively. Specifically, exports to Japan increased by 18.6%, South Korea by 19.1%, Canada by 14.4%, and Mexico by 42.5%. China and the United States continued to be Vietnam's largest trading partners.
 In terms of product categories, the three largest import-export groups are computers, electronic products and components; telephones of all types and components; and machinery, equipment, tools, and spare parts. The total import-export value of these three groups reached US$532 billion, accounting for 54% of the country's total trade turnover, an increase of 49% compared to the same period last year.
 In the context of continued global trade volatility, the Customs sector is implementing directives from the Government, the Prime Minister, and the Ministry of Finance, playing a key role in facilitating trade, ensuring economic security, safeguarding national sovereignty, and supporting the business community in expanding their operations in international markets.
 The milestone of $1 trillion not only reflects the growing scale of import and export activities but also demonstrates the deep integration of the Vietnamese economy. This achievement is the result of the efforts of the business community, the government's management, and the coordination among ministries, sectors, and localities in improving the business environment, expanding markets, and enhancing competitiveness.
 The road ahead still presents many opportunities and challenges. With the growth foundation already built, and the synchronized coordination of the entire system, Vietnam aims to continue improving the quality of trade growth, achieving sustainable development, and affirming its position in the global economy.

|  | 
| The electronics industry is the largest contributor to import and export turnover, with approximately $400 billion as of October 15, 2026. | 
 On October 30th, the Ministry of Industry and Trade held a meeting with major electronics companies to assess the production and import/export situation.
 According to the Import-Export Department, Vietnam's total import and export turnover in the first 10 months of 2026 is estimated to reach over 1,000 billion USD, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period in 2025. Exports are expected to continue strong growth, with an estimated turnover of 499 billion USD in the first 10 months, an increase of 27.4%. 
 Electronics is a sector with a large import value, involving significant participation from FDI enterprises and global production chains. The industry's trade deficit has increased sharply due to its dependence on external supply sources, coupled with the impact of rising raw material prices, leading to increased inventory and production expansion by businesses .  In terms of import and export structure, the electronics industry continues to affirm its position as one of the leading industries, contributing the largest amount of revenue.
 According to data from the Customs Department ( Ministry of Finance ), as of October 15, 2026, the cumulative export value of the two product groups, computers, electronic products and components; and telephones of all types and components, reached US$189.6 billion, accounting for approximately 40% of the total export value.
 Specifically, the group of computers, electronic products and components reached $135.3 billion, a 65% increase compared to the same period in 2025, while telephone components reached $54.3 billion. The increasing demand for artificial intelligence ( AI ) equipment and data centers globally is one of the factors driving the export growth of this product group.
 Despite positive export results, the electronics industry is experiencing a significant trade deficit. Total imports of electronic computers and components; and telephones and components reached $209.7 billion. Of this, imports of computers, electronic products, and components amounted to approximately $201 billion, resulting in a trade deficit of $65.69 billion for this group of goods.
 Although the group of telephones and components recorded a trade surplus of over $45.67 billion, the overall trade balance of the two product groups still showed a deficit of approximately $20 billion.
 According to Mr. Tran Thanh Hai, Deputy Director of the Import-Export Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), Vietnam has become one of the important electronics manufacturing locations in the global supply chain, with the presence of many large corporations such as Samsung , LG, Intel, Foxconn, and Canon...
 Nevertheless, electronics manufacturing in Vietnam still heavily relies on imported components and raw materials, while the localization rate and added value created domestically remain limited.
 The electronics industry's production structure remains highly fragmented. While foreign-invested enterprises (FDI) play a dominant role in manufacturing, assembly, and export, domestic enterprises are primarily involved in component production, supporting industries, and technical services.
 Notably, one of the reasons for the trade deficit is the sharp increase in demand for imported raw materials and components for production. Some types of chips have seen price increases of 300-500%, causing a significant increase in import value even when import volume has not increased proportionally.
 In addition, businesses are increasing their accumulation and stockpiling of raw materials and components to support production plans, while simultaneously expanding factory scale, production lines, and exports. This leads to a demand for importing machinery, equipment, and input materials.
 "In the coming period, attracting FDI needs to focus on key electronics sectors, developing the semiconductor industry, research and development (R&D), enhancing the capacity of supporting industries, strengthening linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic enterprises, diversifying markets and supply sources, aiming to transform Vietnam from a manufacturing and assembly center into a higher-value link in the global electronics supply chain," Mr. Hai emphasized.
 During a meeting with the Vietnam Electronics Business Association and several major import-export businesses in the electronics and semiconductor industry in September 2026, Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc requested the implementation of appropriate solutions to accelerate the production of supporting industries for this sector.
 The Deputy Prime Minister requested a review and update of the list of priority supporting industrial products for the electronics industry, focusing on components and materials with high demand and the potential for localization; and research into support mechanisms based on supply chains and specific products, instead of the current scattered and isolated forms of support.
 Accordingly, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is tasked with leading and coordinating with other ministries, agencies, localities, and associations to develop a program to connect and develop Vietnamese suppliers for domestic and foreign electronics, semiconductor, and technology corporations, based on product chains, technical standards, and business needs.

articles.title: Indonesia - Trade, Agriculture, Manufacturing - Britannica
articles.summary: Indonesia - Trade, Agriculture, Manufacturing  Britannica
articles.full_text:
Indonesia has played a modest role in the world economy since the mid-20th century, and its importance has been considerably less than its size, resources, and geographic position would seem to warrant. The country is a major exporter of crude petroleum and natural gas. In addition, Indonesia is one of the world’s main suppliers of rubber, coffee, cocoa, and palm oil; it also produces a wide range of other commodities, such as sugar, tea, tobacco, copra, and spices (e.g., cloves). Nearly all commodity production comes from large estates. Widespread exploration for deposits of oil and other minerals has resulted in a number of large-scale projects that have contributed substantially to general development funds.
News •
Although Indonesia has remained a major importer of manufactured goods, high technology, and technical skills since the early 1970s, the country’s economic base has shifted from the primary sector to secondary and tertiary industries—manufacturing, trade, and services. Manufacturing surpassed agriculture in terms of contribution to gross domestic product (GDP) in the early 1990s and has continued to be the largest single component of the country’s economy. A significant portion of the national budget has continued to be allocated to agriculture, however; consequently, the country has remained self-sufficient in rice production since the mid-1980s.
During the early years of Indonesia’s independence, economic mismanagement and the subordination of development to political ideals under the “Guided Economy” policy of the country’s first president, Sukarno (1949–66), led to financial chaos and to a serious deterioration in the capital stock. With a major change of economic direction after Suharto assumed power in the mid-1960s, some measure of stability was regained, and the conditions for an orderly policy of rehabilitation and economic development were established.
From 1969 to 1998 a series of five-year plans emphasized the government’s role in developing the economic infrastructure of the country, notably in agriculture, irrigation, transportation, and communications. Thus, the government, together with foreign aid, has been a major force in propelling development in areas where private enterprise has not been immediately forthcoming; the state-owned oil company Pertamina was a product of these government initiatives. In the late 20th century, the emphasis in the public sector tended increasingly toward independent, self-financing state enterprises.
Substantial expansion of the private sector has been evident since the mid-1990s. Prior to that time, growth generally had been confined to a rather small group of conglomerates, most benefiting from the government’s favour. Small business was slower to develop. The deregulation of the capital market in the early 1980s triggered spectacular growth in the stock exchange, but despite the increase in domestic investment, direct participation in the stock market remained limited to a very small group of investors.
Foreign direct investment spiked in the 1990s but rapidly receded in the aftermath of the Asian economic crisis sparked by the collapse of the Thai baht in 1997. The government subsequently inaugurated a four-year national development plan that helped return the economy to its precrisis strength. By 2003 the country was stable enough to allow the expiration of an economic reform program that had been sponsored by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). A new development strategy involving liberalization in some areas and limitation of foreign ownership in others has aimed to establish Indonesia as a fully self-sufficient (swasembada) country in the 21st century.
Agriculture, forestry, and fishing
The consistent monsoon climate and almost even distribution of rainfall in Indonesia make it possible for the same types of crops to be grown throughout the country. Less than one-fifth of the total land surface, however, is devoted to crop cultivation. Most agricultural land is dedicated to rice or to various cash crops. Intensive cultivation is restricted to Java, Bali, Lombok, and certain areas of Sumatra and Celebes. In Java much of the land of the northern coastal and central plains is planted with rice. In the drier section of eastern Java, crops such as corn (maize), cassava, sweet potatoes, peanuts (groundnuts), and soybeans dominate the small farms, although such cash crops as tobacco and coffee also are grown on plantations.
Development in Sumatra and in the outer islands is less intensive and consists primarily of estate-raised cash crops. Sumatra accounts for a major portion of the total area under estate production, and most plantations are located in the island’s northeastern coastal region. Around Medan there are extensive plantations producing tobacco, rubber, palm oil, kapok, tea, cloves, and coffee, none of which is native to the region. Rice, corn, and cassava are grown in the Padang area in the west and around the oil fields near Palembang in the southeast.
Since the late 20th century there has been a shift from rice toward less-demanding subsistence crops, such as cassava. Rice has remained the cornerstone of small-scale agriculture, however, and increased production of it has been an important aim of every economic development plan. The government intervenes in the marketing of rice to maintain production at an economically viable level. Various “mass guidance” (bimbingan massal) schemes to broaden the availability of credit and to promote the use of fertilizers and high-yielding varieties have increased rice output. Although the country is self-sufficient in rice production, there has been a persistent tendency since the late 1990s to import additional rice.
Private enterprises have joined the government in developing Indonesia’s palm oil and sugar industries, as well as its fisheries. Large-scale agribusiness is becoming a more important component of the country’s economy, with increasing government investment. Export of cultivated shrimp from sizable farms in western Java and southern Sumatra has been a boon to middle-sized businesses. Milkfish also are bred through aquaculture. Scad, tuna, and mackerel are the primary products of open-sea fishing.
Indonesia has some of the world’s largest tracts of exploitable tropical forest, especially in Kalimantan and Papua. There are several small areas of deciduous forest and plantations (mostly teak), but most of the trees are evergreen tropical hardwoods. The production of plywood and veneers has become important for both domestic consumption and export. Major timber operations are located primarily in Kalimantan, but logging also occurs on the other large islands; legitimate companies as well as illegal loggers target certain species, such as meranti (a subspecies of the genus Shorea), which yields an easily workable, relatively lightweight reddish wood. Teak is extracted mainly from Java.
Since the 1960s the timber industry has grown rapidly, but it has caused considerable damage through deforestation. Also a threat to the environment are frequent large-scale forest fires, most of which stem from “slash-and-burn” (swidden) subsistence agriculture or government clearing for plantations; these fires not only destroy vast areas of vegetation but also generate haze that frequently reaches as far as Singapore and peninsular Malaysia. Deforestation and air quality issues prompted environmentalists to urge the Indonesian government to curtail clear-cutting of trees, to control burning, and to implement reforestation programs.

“To Canada, Where Tariff Barriers Have Fallen”: Chinese Automakers Step Up Local Push, Seeking Opportunities Amid Spreading Global Protectionism
Authored On
Modified
Chinese automakers, including Geely and BYD, accelerate push into Canada
Canada lowers entry barriers by scrapping steep tariffs on Chinese EVs and introducing an import quota
Chinese companies expand influence in auto markets worldwide, while tariffs and other countermeasures continue
China’s Geely Automobile Holdings has formally announced plans to begin commercial sales in Canada. With barriers to entry lowered after the Canadian government removed steep tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles and introduced a limited import quota, Chinese companies are accelerating efforts to secure local sales networks, infrastructure and production bases. Market observers are watching whether Chinese-made EVs, which have already rapidly expanded their sales presence in Europe, Latin America and Southeast Asia, can also extend their influence in Canada.
Chinese Automakers Set Their Sights on Canada
According to a report on the 15th by British automotive industry outlet inautonews, Geely announced plans to enter the Canadian market in an official press release on the 9th. All dates are local time. The company said it has already established its local organization in Canada and is building a sales and service network ahead of its vehicle launches. “Canada represents an important next step in Geely’s international growth,” said Brian Wu, managing director of Geely Auto Canada. “We will earn consumers’ trust by building strong local partnerships and customer support systems.” Full-scale vehicle sales are scheduled to begin in 2027.
Geely is not the only Chinese automaker preparing to enter Canada. In an interview with Reuters in London last June, BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li said, “We are reviewing which vehicle models to launch in Canada, and actual sales are likely to begin in 2027.” Around the same time, Transport Canada documents also confirmed that BYD had begun procedures to import two passenger vehicle models produced in Shenzhen and Xi’an, China.
Efforts to Secure Infrastructure and Production Bases
BYD is also pursuing plans to build EV charging infrastructure in Canada. Last June, it recruited a business development manager for its “Flash Charging” business in Toronto. The role included △developing a strategy to expand an ultra-fast charging network across Canada △analyzing charging station installation costs and profitability △identifying local partners to handle power grid upgrades, equipment installation and on-site operations △managing charging station construction projects. Flash Charging is an ultra-fast charging technology developed in-house by BYD, with its latest system supporting charging output of up to 1,500 kilowatts (kW). U.S. environmental news outlet The Cool Down (TCD) said, “If Flash Charging technology becomes more widespread, it could ease consumers’ concerns about long-distance driving and charging wait times, while making EV ownership a more practical option for drivers who find it difficult to charge at home.” It added, “Whether BYD can replicate in Canada the charging ecosystem it has built in China will be a key development to watch in the North American EV market.”
Efforts to secure local production bases are also becoming more visible. According to Bloomberg, Patrick Brown, mayor of Brampton, Canada, said last month, “BYD inquired about six months ago about using Stellantis’s Brampton plant to produce buses.” Stellantis had originally been retooling the plant to produce the Jeep Compass sport utility vehicle (SUV), but that work was halted last year when the U.S.-Canada tariff war began. Stellantis subsequently shifted Jeep Compass production to Belvidere, Illinois. In April, Stellantis also held preliminary discussions with Leapmotor, an EV maker based in China’s Zhejiang province, about producing EVs at the Brampton plant.
Removal of Additional Tariffs Lowers Trade Barriers
Chinese automakers’ successive moves into Canada come as the Canadian government eases restrictions on EV imports from China. In January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a trade agreement that included lower tariffs on Chinese-made EVs after meeting with President Xi Jinping in Beijing. Since October 2024, Canada had imposed an additional 100% tariff on Chinese-made EVs on top of the existing 6.1% duty. It agreed to remove that additional tariff and apply the 6.1% most-favored-nation (MFN) rate to up to 49,000 vehicles annually.
The new system took effect on March 1. The Canadian government plans to increase the import quota for Chinese-made EVs, set at 49,000 vehicles in the first year, by 6.5% annually, while allocating 50% of the total quota by 2030 to low-cost EVs with an import price of CAD 35,000 (approximately USD 25,538) or less. The aim is to allow limited market access for Chinese-made EVs while managing the impact on Canada’s domestic auto industry. The Canadian government is also actively encouraging Chinese companies to partner with local businesses to invest in vehicle production facilities and EV supply chains.
Table 1. Canada’s Easing of Import Restrictions on Chinese-Made EVs
| Category | Previous System | Changes | Effective Date and Conditions | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Tariffs | An additional 100% tariff imposed on top of the 6.1% most-favored-nation tariff | A 6.1% tariff applied to vehicles within the import quota, with no additional tariff | Effective March 1, 2026 | 
| Import Quota | No separate country-specific quotas | Imports of 49,000 Chinese-made EVs permitted in the first year, with the quota increasing by 6.5% annually thereafter | The quota year runs from March 1 to the end of February the following year | 
| Allocation for Low-Cost Vehicles | No separate criteria | A portion of the quota allocated to vehicles with an import price of CAD 35,000 or less | Phased increase from 10% in year 2 to 50% in year 5 | 
Chinese EVs Race Ahead in Global Markets
Market observers are watching whether Chinese-made EVs, which have already expanded their sales presence worldwide, can also establish a foothold in Canada. According to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Global EV Outlook 2026, China’s EV exports doubled year on year to more than 2.5 million vehicles last year. Growth has been particularly pronounced in Europe. Data from European automotive market analysis firm Inovev show that Chinese brands sold approximately 795,000 passenger vehicles across 30 European countries last year, up 90% from 417,000 the previous year. Over the same period, Chinese brands’ share of the local new-car market also doubled from about 3% to 6%.
Chinese-made EVs are also penetrating Latin American markets at an accelerating pace. Vehicles produced in China accounted for around 85% of EVs sold in each of Brazil and Mexico last year. Southeast Asia is also emerging as a key market for Chinese EV makers. More than half of the EVs sold in Southeast Asia last year were Chinese-brand vehicles, while local sales of Chinese-made EVs increased by 130% year on year. This sales expansion has continued this year. Last month, global accounting and consulting firm PwC reported that Chinese automakers’ share of the overall new-car market in six major ASEAN countries—Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Singapore—rose from approximately 11% last year to 16% in the first half of this year.
More Countries Impose Steep Tariffs
The problem is that many countries are also stepping up measures to curb Chinese-made EVs. For example, the European Commission conducted an anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese-made EVs for about a year beginning in 2023. In July 2024, it imposed provisional countervailing duties after determining that Chinese government subsidies had distorted competition within the EU market. This was the first large-scale trade sanction against Chinese-made EVs. In October of the same year, following approval by member states, the EU finalized additional tariffs of up to 35.3% on Chinese-made EVs, with rates varying by manufacturer. These duties are imposed on top of the existing 10% vehicle import tariff and were set to apply for five years from October 30, 2024.
Last December, Mexico also approved legislation imposing tariffs of up to 50% on approximately 1,400 products, including vehicles, auto parts, steel and textiles, imported from countries without free trade agreements (FTAs), including China. The measures took full effect on January 1 this year. Tariffs of up to 50% apply to finished vehicles, while many other products face rates of 35% or less. The Brazilian government has been gradually raising import tariffs on electrified vehicles since January 2024. As of July 1, it raised import tariffs on fully assembled battery electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and conventional hybrids to a uniform 35%.

 Exports increased sharply, with the processing industry playing a leading role.

 Aiming for high growth and increasing technological content.

SEMIEXPO Vietnam 2026 is expected to bring together more than 200 exhibitors, promoting direct connections between Vietnamese businesses and leading global semiconductor corporations.
On October 29th, in Ho Chi Minh City, the Southeast Asian Semiconductor Association (SEMI SEA), in collaboration with the National Innovation Center (NIC), the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Science and Technology, and other partners, held a press conference on SEMIEXPO Vietnam 2026. This event marks a shift from promoting and introducing technology to fostering substantive cooperation, creating opportunities for Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in the global semiconductor supply chain.
SEMIEXPO Vietnam 2026 is the leading large-scale international semiconductor industry exhibition in Vietnam. It is an important international forum bringing together the entire value chain of the microelectronics and semiconductor industry.
Connecting Vietnamese businesses with the global semiconductor supply chain.
Speaking at the press conference, Ms. Linda Tan, President of SEMI Southeast Asia, said that SEMIEXPO Vietnam 2026 will continue to expand in scale and level of participation from the international semiconductor community. The exhibition is expected to feature over 200 booths and more than 100 participating companies, an increase of approximately 30% compared to the previous year. The event is also expected to attract delegates from 24 countries and territories, an increase of approximately 20%.
This is the third time SEMIEXPO has been held in Vietnam and the first time in Ho Chi Minh City, following two previous editions in Hanoi . According to Ms. Linda Tan, the choice of Ho Chi Minh City reflects the potential of a technology, manufacturing, and innovation hub, and demonstrates the growing interest of international partners in the Vietnamese semiconductor market.

With a network of over 4,000 member companies worldwide, SEMI aims to become a bridge between domestic suppliers and international customers, between research and training institutions and businesses, thereby transforming cooperation potential into concrete economic activities.
The highlight of this year's SEMIEXPO is the Supplier Search Program (SSP), designed to directly connect Vietnamese businesses with international buyers through one-on-one meetings.
Linda Tan emphasized that the program not only facilitates businesses in showcasing their production capabilities but also helps them access technical requirements, procurement standards, and build long-term cooperative relationships. International companies such as Besi, Lam Research, and TechInsights were introduced to participate in networking activities, opening up opportunities to understand the actual needs of the market.
Notably, the program targets suppliers who meet the standards, rather than simply organizing introductory meetings. This places a demand on Vietnamese businesses to improve their technological capabilities, quality management, and ability to meet the stringent standards of the semiconductor industry.
From the perspective of regulatory bodies, Mr. Vo Xuan Hoai, Deputy Director of the National Innovation Center (NIC) under the Ministry of Finance, stated that Vietnam's semiconductor ecosystem is developing rapidly. While in 2023 there were approximately 50 businesses operating in related fields nationwide, that number has now increased to nearly 100, with over 50 of them focusing on chip design.

According to the Deputy Director of the National Innovation Center (NIC) under the Ministry of Finance, along with the increase in the number of businesses, Vietnam is receiving attention from major technology corporations. Notably, the NIC has worked directly with ASML to promote connections between Vietnamese businesses and the corporation's supplier network.
Besides ASML, companies such as Lam Research, KLA, Coherent, and Onsemi were also mentioned in the plan to expand cooperation. These are positive signs for Vietnam's supporting industries, as opportunities to participate in the value chain are not limited to design, packaging, or testing, but also extend to equipment, materials, and related technical services.
However, access to international corporations does not automatically mean the ability to become a supplier immediately. To translate these connections into commercial contracts, domestic businesses need to demonstrate stable production capacity, meet quality requirements, and gradually participate in higher value-added stages of the process.
In this context, SEMIEXPO Vietnam 2026 is expected to become a platform supporting domestic businesses in expanding their markets, finding partners, and gradually improving their position in the global semiconductor supply chain.
Completing the semiconductor ecosystem and developing human resources.
Along with supply chain connectivity, infrastructure, institutions, and human resources were identified by delegates as crucial conditions for Vietnam to enhance its competitiveness in the semiconductor industry.
Mr. Nguyen Huu Yen, Deputy Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Science and Technology, said that after expanding its development space, the city is focusing on investing in transportation infrastructure, social infrastructure, and planning concentrated digital technology zones to create conditions for attracting investment capital into high technology, especially semiconductors.
Alongside infrastructure development, Ho Chi Minh City is continuing to build and refine policies and mechanisms in the field of science and technology, aiming to remove bottlenecks, improve the investment environment, and support businesses in implementing new projects or expanding operations.
According to the Deputy Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Science and Technology, the city also focuses on linking businesses, research institutes, and training facilities; implementing programs to improve skills, retrain human resources, and create conditions for students to access the real production environment from an early age. This is considered a solution to prepare human resources to meet the development needs of the industry in the coming years.
From the perspective of a business developing industrial infrastructure, Ms. Tran Thi Hong Minh, Deputy General Director of Becamex Group, believes that developing the semiconductor industry is not just about attracting investment or building factories, but requires creating a synchronized ecosystem, including modern industrial infrastructure, stable and green energy, high-quality human resources, research, testing, and technology transfer.
This is also the direction Becamex is pursuing in its transition from simply developing industrial infrastructure to building an integrated ecosystem of industry, technology, training, and innovation, through the Becamex - VSIP network.
Notably, Becamex is promoting the connection between training and business needs through the Eastern International University, Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City, the Vietnamese-German International University, and international partners such as A*STAR of Singapore and the Fraunhofer Institute of Germany.

These platforms are connected to the development orientation of the science and technology urban area in the North of Ho Chi Minh City, aiming to strengthen the links between research, training, testing, and technology application, gradually improving the capacity of Vietnamese businesses to participate in the supply chain.
In the field of training, Dr. Huynh Phu Minh Cuong, Deputy Head of the Science and Technology Department, Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City, emphasized that the demand for semiconductor human resources is not limited to university level. International businesses increasingly need a team of experts with master's and doctoral degrees, capable of participating in research and solving in-depth technological problems.
According to Mr. Cuong, the Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City has developed specialized training programs in integrated circuit design, chip packaging technology, and semiconductor component manufacturing, with a scale he mentioned of approximately 1,000 undergraduate students, 200 master's students, and more than 20 doctoral candidates each year.
In particular, the unit is finalizing the National-level Shared Integrated Circuit Design Laboratory, aiming to combine training with research, testing, and collaboration with businesses. In the next phase, this facility is expected to further develop its semiconductor component research and manufacturing capabilities, creating conditions for the formation of innovative projects and technology startups.
These directions indicate that the development of Vietnam's semiconductor industry requires closer linkages between the State, businesses, research institutes, and training institutions. If market connectivity is implemented in parallel with improving industrial capacity, infrastructure, and human resources, Vietnam will have a stronger foundation to translate its investment-attracting advantages into substantial participation in the global semiconductor value chain.
According to the Organizing Committee, SEMIEXPO Vietnam 2026 will take place on December 3-4 at the Thiskyhall Sala Convention Center, Ho Chi Minh City, with the theme "Beyond Aspirations: Shaping the Future of Vietnamese Semiconductors". Besides the exhibition space, the program includes specialized conferences, business networking activities, professional exchanges, and discussion sessions on trends in the semiconductor industry.
