According to estimates, Vietnam's total import and export turnover in the first 10 months of 2026 reached US$1,010.6 billion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period in 2025, officially surpassing the US$1 trillion mark. In October alone, import and export turnover is estimated at US$122.2 billion, an increase of 47.6% compared to the same period last year.
 Notably, exports continued to grow strongly, with estimated turnover reaching $499 billion in the first 10 months, an increase of 27.4%, creating positive momentum to achieve and surpass the export growth target of 15-16% for the whole year of 2026.
 Export growth occurred in both the domestic and foreign direct investment (FDI) sectors, with processed industrial goods continuing to play a leading role, accounting for 87.4% of total export turnover. Exports also recorded positive growth in many major markets such as China, the United States , the EU, South Korea, and ASEAN.
 Regarding the trade balance, October is estimated to have a trade surplus of $6.8 billion, marking the second consecutive month of surplus and bringing the cumulative trade deficit for the first 10 months down to approximately $12.7 billion. This result shows that import and export activities continue to maintain positive growth momentum, affirming the important role of goods trade in economic growth. 
 Imports and exports achieved high performance in the first 10 months of 2026.
 Currently, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is developing a draft strategy for goods import and export until 2030, with a vision to 2045. According to the draft, the goal is to achieve an average annual growth rate of 15-16% in goods export turnover during the 2026-2030 period; and an average annual growth rate of 12-13% in imports. The trade balance aims for a sustainable surplus, with the proportion of export surplus to total export turnover averaging 3-6% during this period. By 2045, Vietnam strives to be among the top 10 countries with the largest export and import turnover in the world; with a trade surplus ratio of 7-10%.
 One of the key objectives is to enhance the role of domestic enterprises and increase the processing and technological content in exports. Accordingly, the proportion of export turnover from the domestic enterprise sector in the total national export turnover is targeted to reach approximately 28-30% by 2030, increasing to 38-40% by 2045. The proportion of processed or refined goods in the total export turnover is expected to reach 89-90% by 2030 and over 92% by 2045. The proportion of high-tech product exports in the total value of processed and manufactured goods exports is targeted to reach approximately 50% by 2030 and over 55% by 2045.
 Regarding trade scale, the draft presents growth scenarios up to 2030. In the medium scenario, export turnover is expected to reach US$953.7 billion by 2030; the high scenario targets US$1,041.1 billion, while the low scenario is US$765 billion. These scenarios indicate the need to expand export scale in conjunction with improving domestic production capacity, developing processing and manufacturing industries, and increasing the competitiveness of goods.
 In the fourth quarter, the Ministry of Industry and Trade identified key areas for boosting exports, diversifying markets, and improving compliance capacity. This includes focusing on effectively utilizing signed Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), expanding into new markets; and enhancing early warning capabilities regarding trade defense cases, tariff barriers, green standards, traceability, and rules of origin.
 Simultaneously, support businesses in improving product quality, building brands, and ensuring transparency in the supply chain. articles.title: Vietnam’s export outlook holding firm - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Vietnam’s export outlook holding firm  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Hanoi (VNA) – Vietnam’s export outlook is holding firm despite unpredictable global trade, supported by stronger manufacturing capacity, higher realised foreign direct investment and a widening web of free trade agreements (FTAs). 
Opening up more opportunities 
Vietnam formally signed a FTA with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) in mid-October, after 14 years of negotiations. The deal, known as VEFTA, opens a new chapter aimed at deepening economic, investment and trade ties with highly developed markets. 
“The four EFTA markets do not import much Vietnamese seafood at present, but having a free trade agreement will make two-way trade easier and widen cooperation between Vietnamese companies and partners strong in fishing, processing and seafood technology,” said Deputy Secretary General of the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers (VASEP) Le Hang. 
Switzerland stands out among EFTA markets for Vietnamese seafood, with high purchasing power and demand for quality, sustainably produced goods with transparent origins. Vietnam has a particular edge in eco-friendly shrimp, especially mangrove forest shrimp raised under the mangrove canopy. 
The VEFTA is also expected to open more doors for tra fish, processed tuna and other added-value seafood. The opportunity goes beyond shipping more goods, with room to attract investment, absorb technology and move into higher-value stages of the production chain. 
Once in force, the VEFTA will create more export opportunities and deepen seafood supply chain cooperation for Vietnamese companies. Tariff preferences under the deal will also give consumers more chances to buy quality goods at good prices, notably Norwegian salmon, whose import duties now 10% for whole fish and 15% for fillets, will fall to zero when the VEFTA takes effect. 
Vietnam’s exports totalled 463.7 billion USD as of October 15, up 25.9% from the same period last year and far above the 15-16% target. 
Le Hoang Tai, Deputy Director of the Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency at the Ministry of Industry and Trade, said Vietnam continues to attract shifting production as global supply chains restructure. That gives local companies room to take a deeper role in international manufacturing networks and expand exports of electronics, machinery, components, apparel, wooden furniture and processed industrial goods. 
“Macroeconomic stability and deep economic links through 17 FTAs in force offer a major opportunity to evolve from a simple processing link into a key production and supply hub with higher value added”, Tai said. 
Capital flowing into electronics, artificial intelligence and semiconductors from global technology groups is turning Vietnam into a hi-tech manufacturing hub of growing capacity. Electronics exports could contribute about 250 billion USD to Vietnam’s exports in 2026, according to estimates. 
Alongside markets already covered by FTAs, closer economic and trade ties with countries in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Latin America and other emerging markets are adding outlets for Vietnamese goods. That helps companies reduce reliance on a few traditional markets. 
Stronger production base 
Vietnamese goods are increasingly present in global markets, particularly electronics, textile and garments, agricultural products, and timber and wood products. But tighter requirements on the environment, emissions, raw material sourcing and supply chain responsibility are piling on pressure, forcing companies to revamp production processes and better meet international standards. 
Tran Thanh Hai, Deputy Director of the Export-Import Department at the Ministry of Industry and Trade, said companies that stop at simple processing and assembly will struggle to withstand increasingly strict technical barriers. Real-world trade has already shown the risks when policies change. 
Global trade trends in the coming time will favour products that can prove clear origin, use sustainable materials, save energy and meet environmental standards, giving them better access to customers in markets with high import requirements. 
Competitiveness in global trade no longer rests on price and production scale alone. Meeting standards, providing transparent information and ensuring supply chain sustainability are increasingly the conditions for companies to keep markets and win more orders. 
Ito Group Holdings Pte. Ltd. has made Vietnam its manufacturing hub since 2012, said its Chairman Peter James Opdahl. The group is now building a new 12,000 sq.m factory in Ho Chi Minh City’s Linh Trung Export Processing Zone to make equipment used in manufacturing across many industries. 
According to him, Vietnam’s appeal goes beyond market access through FTAs to an increasingly clear role in regional production networks. To draw more quality projects and amplify spillover effects, the country needs to keep improving its industrial ecosystem, raise domestic supply capacity and develop technical talent, helping Vietnamese companies widen their international connections. 
Vietnam’s trade outlook for 2026 remains upbeat, with a fairly realistic target of as much as 1.2 trillion USD in total export-import turnover and staying among the world’s 15 largest trading powers./.

Technology and electronics corporations, including Foxconn, are expanding their manufacturing operations in northern Vietnam. This trend strengthens Vietnam's position as an alternative to China in the global supply chain, particularly in the electronics and high-tech sectors.

Tìm hiểu lịch sử
While Vietnam benefits from the shift in supply chains and investment flows into manufacturing, Indonesia's economic growth remains around 5%.

articles.full_text:
Vietnam is poised to overtake Indonesia in nominal gross domestic product (GDP) per capita this year, as rapid economic expansion, foreign investment and rising exports strengthen its position among Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing economies.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts that Vietnam’s nominal GDP per capita will increase by 8.9% in 2026 to US$5,259, almost doubling its level over the past decade.
This would put Vietnam ahead of Indonesia, whose GDP per capita is projected at US$5,153, making Vietnam the fifth-ranked country in ASEAN by this measure, behind Thailand.
Vietnam’s economic momentum has been supported by its emergence as an alternative manufacturing base to China, particularly in high-tech industries such as semiconductors and electronics.
The government has set a target of achieving economic growth of at least 10% in 2026. Real GDP expanded by 9.95% in the third quarter.
Mai Fujita, a senior researcher at the Institute of Developing Economies, attributed much of the momentum to government spending.
"Proactive public investment is a key factor supporting economic growth," she noted.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows rose by 12% year on year to US$21.1 billion during the January-September period. Major international manufacturers, including Taiwan-based electronics giant Foxconn and South Korea's Samsung, have continued expanding their production operations in the country.
Meanwhile, newly registered investment projects surged by 76% to US$50.3 billion, pointing to strong potential for further investment in the years ahead.
Vietnam’s export sector has also recorded strong growth, with shipments rising by 25% year on year to US$434 billion during the first nine months of 2026.
Several South Korean companies, including Samsung Electronics, have established manufacturing facilities in Vietnam to produce smartphones and other electronic products for international markets.
US trade statistics also show that the country’s goods trade deficit with Vietnam reached US$160 billion in the first eight months of the year, surpassing its deficits with both China and Mexico.
Indonesia, meanwhile, has attracted substantial investment in its electric vehicle (EV) industry, but its economy continues to expand at around 5% annually.
One concern is that investment in the sector has yet to generate sufficient employment or significantly increase household incomes. A weaker rupiah has also weighed on Indonesia’s GDP per capita when measured in US dollars.
Vietnam is now setting its sights on raising GDP per capita to US$8,500 by 2030, a level comparable to Thailand’s current figure.
Thailand, however, is experiencing much slower economic expansion, with real GDP growth of only around 2% a year. High household debt is among the factors holding back economic activity.
Despite Vietnam’s strong performance, international financial institutions remain cautious about its ambitious growth targets.
Both the IMF and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) project that Vietnam’s economy will expand by around 7.5% in 2027, falling short of the government’s 10% growth ambition.
Fujita stressed that Vietnam must place greater emphasis on sustainable economic development rather than relying solely on short-term expansion.
"Vietnam needs to make efforts focused on long-term growth, such as developing human resources and technology, alongside infrastructure investment that can stimulate growth in the short term," she said.

articles.title: Imports and exports surpass $1 trillion: Behind this historic milestone lies the challenge of strengthening Vietnamese businesses. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Imports and exports surpass $1 trillion: Behind this historic milestone lies the challenge of strengthening Vietnamese businesses.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
For the first time in history, Vietnam's import and export turnover exceeded US$1 trillion in October 2026, two months ahead of the end of the year. This milestone demonstrates the ever-expanding scale of the economy's trade.
However, with imports growing faster than exports, and the FDI sector accounting for nearly 78% of total trade turnover, there is a need to improve production capacity, the ability to participate in supply chains, and the value that domestic businesses can retain.
Trade volume is increasing rapidly, but imports are growing even more sharply.
On October 29, 2026, the total value of Vietnam's goods exports and imports reached approximately US$1,001.3 billion. This marks the first time the economy has surpassed the US$1 trillion mark, while there are still more than two months left in 2026.
According to updated figures from the Customs Department, export turnover reached US$493.64 billion, an increase of US$105.56 billion, or 27.2%, compared to the same period last year. Meanwhile, imports reached US$507.66 billion, an increase of US$138.72 billion, or 37.6%. Thus, the import growth rate was 10.4 percentage points higher than the export growth rate, bringing the trade balance at the time of statistics to a deficit of approximately US$14.02 billion.
From a manufacturing perspective, the sharp increase in imports may reflect the growing demand for raw materials, components, machinery, and equipment for production and export activities. This is characteristic of Vietnam's production model, where many industries remain significantly dependent on foreign input supplies.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
However, when the rate of import growth exceeds that of export growth, the issue arises not only from the scale of trade but also from the ability to proactively secure domestic supply. If production increases but the majority of raw materials, components, and technology still have to be imported, the value created and retained in the economy will depend significantly on the supply capacity of domestic businesses.
Looking back at its development, Vietnam's trade expansion has been increasingly rapid. In 2007, total import and export turnover first reached 100 billion USD. By 2011, this figure exceeded 200 billion USD; in 2015 it reached 300 billion USD; in 2019 it reached 500 billion USD; in 2022 it reached 700 billion USD; and in 2025 it is projected to surpass 900 billion USD.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Notably, from $351.38 billion in 2016, total import and export turnover increased to $929.92 billion in 2025, approximately 2.65 times higher. During the period 2016-2025, the average growth rate reached 11% per year. Vietnam currently ranks 18th in the world in exports, 20th in imports, and second in ASEAN in total trade turnover, after Singapore .
Surpassing the $1 trillion mark also demonstrates the increasing openness of the economy to trade. Vietnam currently has trade relations with 237 countries and territories, with 36 export markets and 31 import markets exceeding $1 billion in trade value.
This is a significant advantage in the context of a constantly fluctuating global trade environment marked by geopolitical conflicts, energy costs, and changes in the trade policies of major economies. However, greater openness also means that the economy needs to be more adaptable to external fluctuations.
FDI accounts for nearly 78%: The challenge of elevating the position of domestic businesses.
One notable aspect of the import-export structure is the disparity between the FDI sector and domestic enterprises. According to Customs data, the FDI sector achieved approximately US$778 billion in import-export turnover, accounting for 77.5% of total turnover and increasing by 37% compared to the same period. Meanwhile, the domestic enterprise sector achieved approximately US$223 billion, an increase of 16%.
You may also like
Thus, the majority of Vietnam's international trade activities are still linked to the foreign-invested enterprise sector. This is a result of attracting investment, developing production centers, and participating more deeply in global supply chains.
The electronics, telephone, machinery, and equipment sectors clearly demonstrate the role of the FDI area. Three product groups – computers, electronic products and components; telephones and components; and other machinery, equipment, tools, and spare parts – achieved a total import and export turnover of approximately US$532 billion. These product groups account for a large proportion of the trade structure and experienced strong growth compared to the same period last year.
The growth of these product groups helps Vietnam consolidate its position in the international production and supply network. However, the large proportion of some product sectors also necessitates enhanced resilience as the global technology market, consumer demand, and supply chains change.
For domestic businesses, the challenge is not only expanding production scale to participate in exports but also gradually becoming more deeply involved in high value-added stages. If Vietnamese businesses mainly focus on processing, labor supply, or low-value stages, the majority of the product's value can still be concentrated in businesses that hold technology, design, branding, and distribution networks.
This also explains why increasing the proportion of domestic enterprises in export activities is becoming a crucial requirement in future trade orientations.
According to the draft Strategy for Import and Export of Goods until 2030, with a vision to 2045, developed by the Ministry of Industry and Trade , the proportion of export turnover from domestic enterprises is targeted to reach approximately 28-30% by 2030 and increase to 38-40% by 2045. The draft also aims to increase the proportion of processed or refined goods in total export turnover to 89-90% by 2030.
These goals highlight the need to shift from growth heavily reliant on scaling up to improving the quality and value of goods. To achieve this, domestic businesses need increased capacity in technology, capital, management, production standards, and the ability to connect with multinational corporations.
More importantly, attracting FDI needs to go hand in hand with promoting linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic businesses. When Vietnamese businesses can supply components, raw materials, technical services, and participate in more demanding production stages, the spillover effects of foreign investment on the economy will be more pronounced.
Customs reforms facilitate trade flows.
With the rapid increase in import and export activities, the Customs sector is facing the need to innovate its management methods, not only to handle the ever-increasing volume of documents but also to shorten customs clearance time, reduce costs for businesses, and improve the efficiency of goods control.
According to the results of the third quarter of 2026 by the Customs Department, out of a total of 171 administrative procedures implemented by the agency, 96 procedures are provided with full online public services, 49 procedures are partially online, and 26 procedures provide information online. Between June 15th and September 14th, 2026, the Customs Department received over 29.27 million dossiers, almost all of which were processed online. This is an important basis for reducing paperwork, limiting direct contact, and speeding up the processing of procedures.
Notably, the Customs system has received and processed 44 types of electronic documents, supporting automatic verification with information on the declaration form. The application of artificial intelligence ( AI ) technology in converting document information also contributes to reducing data entry operations, minimizing errors, and reducing printing costs for businesses.
You may also like
Along with document digitization, a centralized customs clearance model will be piloted from June 1, 2026, at the Customs Sub-Department of Region III ( Hai Phong ). Under this model, the receipt and inspection of documents are centralized at a single point instead of being processed in a decentralized manner across multiple customs units at border gates and outside the border. Initial results show that the average customs clearance time has decreased by approximately 12% compared to May 2026 and 14% compared to the first quarter of 2026.
These changes indicate that customs reform is gradually shifting from simplifying individual procedures to reorganizing management processes based on data and technology. The Customs sector is also continuing to build an information technology system to implement digital customs, researching the application of AI in operations, and preparing the conditions for deploying smart border gates.
For import and export businesses, the benefits lie not only in reduced paperwork but also in the ability to shorten delivery times, limit warehousing and storage costs, and be more proactive in production and business planning.
However, the effectiveness of reforms should not be judged solely by the number of procedures moved online or the number of electronic documents received. What businesses are more concerned about is the total time to complete procedures, warehousing, storage, transportation, specialized inspection costs, and the predictability of goods delivery times.
In particular, for small and medium-sized enterprises, the costs incurred during import and export can significantly impact their competitiveness. Therefore, customs reform needs to be implemented in conjunction with reforms to specialized inspection procedures, development of logistics infrastructure, data connectivity between management agencies, and improvement of service quality at border gates and seaports.
The $1 trillion milestone therefore not only reflects the growing scale of Vietnam's trade but also places new demands on the quality of growth. The next phase is not simply about continuing to increase import

articles.title: Vietnamese exporters face dual challenge over power supply - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnamese exporters face dual challenge over power supply  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Ensuring an adequate power supply remains critical as Vietnam's manufacturing and exports expand rapidly. However, some companies in global supply chains must also meet requirements on renewable electricity use and emissions. A draft amendment to Vietnam’s Electricity Law, now under consideration by the National Assembly, seeks to refine mechanisms to address these needs.
On October 20, at a working session of the National Assembly, the country's legislature, Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung presented a proposal to amend and supplement several provisions of the Electricity Law. The draft focuses on resolving bottlenecks in power generation and grid investment, while refining the framework for direct power purchase agreements (DPPAs) and renewable energy certificates.
The proposals come as businesses’ electricity needs evolve. National Assembly member Trinh Tu Anh, representing Lam Dong province, said many companies, particularly those participating in international supply chains, need not only reliable electricity at competitive prices but also proof of energy origin, renewable electricity usage, and emissions generated during production.
This presents the power sector with two parallel challenges: ensuring sufficient electricity to support economic growth and enabling businesses to access clean power and verify its use to meet customer requirements.
Reliable power supply remains an immediate priority
Vietnam’s manufacturing and export activities continued to expand strongly in the first nine months of 2026. Merchandise exports reached $434.3 billion, up 24.5% from a year earlier, according to the National Statistics Office. Industrial production rose 12.3%, while manufacturing and processing output increased 12.9%.
The expansion in manufacturing has been accompanied by a substantial rise in electricity demand.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade reported that commercial electricity consumption nationwide reached 237.19 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in the first nine months, up 9.66% year-on-year. Industry and construction accounted for 122.18 billion kWh, an increase of 8.32%, representing around 51.5% of total electricity sales.
Accounting for more than half of consumption, industry and construction remain the largest electricity-consuming sectors. For factories, a stable power supply is essential to keep production lines running, operate equipment and meet delivery schedules.
The ministry said the power system operated safely and reliably during the nine-month period, meeting demand from businesses and households. Maintaining supply over the longer term, however, will require coordinated development of generation capacity, transmission networks and grid dispatch capabilities.
According to Vietnam Electricity (EVN), total electricity generated and imported across the system reached 265.79 billion kWh in the first nine months. Coal-fired power contributed 132.63 billion kWh, or 49.9%, while hydropower generated 68.48 billion kWh, or 25.8%. Renewable energy sources, as classified by EVN, supplied 33.6 billion kWh, accounting for 12.6%. Gas-fired power contributed 20.48 billion kWh, while electricity imports totalled 10.3 billion kWh.
Hydropower output fell nearly 9% from a year earlier amid hydrological conditions affected by the El Niño phenomenon.
By contrast, coal- and gas-fired power together increased their share of total generation and imports to 57.6%, from 53.9% a year earlier, despite growth in other renewable energy sources. The shift towards a greater share of fossil fuels adds pressure to greenhouse gas emissions at a time when environmental requirements are becoming increasingly linked to manufacturing and export activities.
At the "Clean Energy for a New Era of Growth" forum held in Hanoi on October 27, Mai Duy Thien, chairman of the Vietnam Clean Energy Association, stressed the need to consider energy development in the context of economic growth and national competitiveness.
Clean energy development would not only help diversify supply but also enable businesses to adapt to increasingly stringent environmental standards, he said. This highlights the need to address energy security and the transition to cleaner electricity in parallel.
Clean electricity becomes a gateway to global supply chains
Renewable electricity requirements are already being incorporated into the supply-chain policies of multinational corporations, rather than remaining a trend expected to emerge in the future.
According to its 2026 Environmental Progress Report, Apple has incorporated a requirement for 100% renewable electricity into its Supplier Code of Conduct. The company requires its direct manufacturing supply chain to use 100% renewable electricity for Apple-related production by 2030.
According to the U.S. technology company, electricity consumption at supplier factories is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions across its supply chain. Switching to renewable power is therefore a key component of its 2030 carbon neutrality goal.
Environmental requirements are also being considered as part of trade policy. In the United States, the proposed Clean Competition Act, introduced in Congress in December 2025, would establish a carbon border adjustment mechanism based on the emissions intensity of goods.
Meanwhile, the European Union entered the definitive phase of its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) on January 1, 2026, with the purchase and surrender of CBAM certificates scheduled to follow a phased timeline beginning in 2027. The mechanism covers products in six sectors: iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen.
Under the scheme, EU importers must fulfil obligations linked to emissions embedded in covered goods. Carbon costs could affect purchasing prices and the competitiveness of foreign producers, making emissions management an economic consideration as well as an environmental responsibility for businesses.
In Vietnam, demand for renewable electricity has already translated into actual transactions.
On June 1, 2026, Samsung Electronics Vietnam Thai Nguyen (SEVT) announced that it had implemented a direct power purchase agreement through the national grid, becoming the first corporate customer to complete a transaction under the DPPA mechanism.
The electricity supplied under the agreement comes from the TTC Duc Hue 2 solar power plant in Tay Ninh province, with expected output of around 70 million kWh a year.
The government established the DPPA framework under Decree 57/2025/ND-CP, which was subsequently amended and supplemented by Decree 243/2026/ND-CP. Current regulations have expanded participation to eligible electricity retailers operating in qualifying industrial and economic zones, creating additional arrangements for industrial customers to purchase renewable electricity.
Samsung’s case demonstrates that demand for renewable power has moved beyond commitments to actual transactions. It also raises questions about how the DPPA mechanism can be expanded to give more manufacturers access to clean electricity.
However, transactions conducted through the national grid require participants to account for network usage, dispatch, reserve capacity and other system services. How these costs are calculated and allocated directly affects companies’ overall electricity bills, as well as the interests of customers that do not participate in DPPAs.
This was among the issues the National Assembly’s Committee on Science, Technology and Environment called for clarification in its appraisal report on the draft Electricity Law amendments on October 20. The committee said DPPA participants should fulfil their cost obligations in full to prevent unreasonable cost transfers to other customers.
Beyond access to renewable electricity, businesses also need tools to verify the environmental attributes of the power they consume. Renewable energy certificates (RECs) serve this purpose, but their trading and use require reliable registration, verification and traceability mechanisms.
The draft amendments seek to establish a more complete legal framework for the REC market. The appraisal committee has called for clear rules on certificate ownership, trading and cancellation after use to prevent the same environmental attributes from being claimed more than once.
The issues under consideration therefore go beyond expanding the right to purchase renewable electricity. They also concern the overall cost of transactions and businesses’ ability to demonstrate that they use clean power - conditions that matter to companies seeking to meet environmental commitments made to international partners.
Reuters recently reported that the U.S.-China tariff war had helped accelerate the relocation of manufacturing to Vietnam. The expansion of export-oriented production has brought rising electricity demand. However, Reuters warned that the high share of coal-fired power in Vietnam’s electricity mix could pose an emissions challenge as international buyers increasingly scrutinize the carbon footprints of their supply chains.
For domestic companies seeking deeper integration into global supply chains, the ability to secure reliable electricity, manage emissions and meet partners’ environmental standards is likely to become increasingly important. These factors could increasingly influence the competitiveness of Vietnamese businesses as environmental requirements across global supply chains become more stringent.

articles.full_text:
| A factory of Toan Cau Mechanical Engineering Company in Giang Điền Industrial Park, Đồng Nai City. — VNA/VNS Photo | 
HÀ NỘI — The Vietnam–European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Free Trade Agreement (VEFTA), signed on October 18, is expected to offer Vietnamese mechanical engineering and electronics businesses an opportunity to move beyond low-value assembly and integrate more deeply into global high-tech supply chains, while gaining access to advanced European manufacturing technologies.
While Việt Nam’s free trade agreements often draw attention for their benefits to traditional exports such as agricultural products, seafood and textiles, electronics and mechanical components hold significant strategic potential in trade with EFTA, comprising Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
Unlike mass-market destinations, EFTA markets have strong demand for microchips, specialised electronic equipment, medical devices and precision-engineered products.
Experts from the Centre for World Trade Organisation (WTO) and International Trade under the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI) said VEFTA’s strong tariff cuts could give Vietnamese industrial goods a significant cost advantage. However, strict rules of origin and European technical standards demand manufacturers maintain rigorous quality control and meet micrometre-level precision requirements.
Rather than simply assembling products under foreign brands, Vietnamese businesses should focus on supplying “Make in Vietnam” components to core technology supply chains in Northern and Western Europe, experts said.
Nguyễn Đức Trung, chairman of Vietnam HBT Precise Mechanical JSC, said exporting aluminium profiles and machine components to EFTA markets requires much stricter standards than in other Asian markets. For example, Swiss partners demand precise technical tolerances, transparent material-origin records and data on carbon emissions from machining.
While challenging, meeting these requirements and securing approved-supplier status can help businesses reduce price pressures, he noted.
EFTA member countries are also major suppliers of specialised machinery, smart industrial equipment, autonomous robots and basic chemicals. High import tariffs have made European technologies expensive for Vietnamese supporting-industry enterprises, forcing some to rely on older equipment or machinery from secondary markets. The full removal of tariffs on these products under VEFTA is expected to ease access to core technologies at more reasonable operating costs.
Trương Thị Chí Bình, vice chairwoman and secretary general of the Vietnam Association for Supporting Industries (VASI), said the greatest benefit Việt Nam’s mechanical engineering sector should seek from EFTA is access to core technologies, particularly advanced CNC machining systems.
Only by mastering manufacturing capabilities using world-class equipment could Vietnamese mechanical engineering firms achieve production autonomy rather than remain stuck in low-value contract manufacturing, she added.
Imports of modern production lines, coupled with EFTA investment in automation and green logistics in Việt Nam, will intensify domestic competition, pushing local supporting-industry companies to upgrade capabilities and standardise processes from input materials to final machining, Binh noted.
According to Bình, Switzerland set a global benchmark for precision engineering, meaning Vietnamese suppliers must improve machining accuracy and quality management. Without meeting stringent tolerances, tariff preferences alone would not translate into multimillion-dollar orders.
Đỗ Phước Tống, a representative of the HCM City Association of Mechanical - Electrical Enterprises, said supplying components to EFTA partners offers a fair and transparent business environment in which quality is highly valued and labour costs are not unfairly squeezed. The resulting profit margins could generate healthy cash flow for domestic firms to reinvest in their own research and development (R&D) centres.
VEFTA opens up opportunities for Vietnamese technology and mechanical engineering firms to access a market with some of the world’s highest standards. To maximise the new-generation agreement’s benefits, businesses need to boost R&D activities and digitalise operations. Strengthening capabilities and mastering technology will be key to upgrading Việt Nam’s electronics and precision engineering sectors and strongly integrating them into global high-tech supply chains. — VNA/VNS

articles.title: China Is Building Its Way Around Europe’s EV Tariffs - Asociación Almendrón
articles.summary: China Is Building Its Way Around Europe’s EV Tariffs  Asociación Almendrón
articles.full_text:
In recent years, Europe’s auto industry has reeled from the influx of low-cost, high-quality Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Even as Brussels imposes tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, their market share only continues to grow. As of December, more than 9 percent of all new automobiles sold in Europe were made in China, with some estimates expecting Chinese EVs to account for roughly 20 percent of the Western European market by 2028.
Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs reflect a common Western view that high-value Chinese products are competitive in global markets largely because of state subsidies. To be sure, China’s EV industry has benefited immensely from Beijing’s subsidies, easy credit, and tax relief. That explanation, however, is far too narrow and risks severely underestimating the scale of the challenge ahead.
The more consequential story—that will likely make Chinese EVs even more competitive in the near future—is Beijing’s evolving approach to overseas industrial policy. At the core of this approach is an increasingly coordinated model of public- and private-sector activity.
State-owned enterprises (SOE) lay the groundwork for favorable investment environments abroad by undertaking massive infrastructure projects and securing access to strategic resources. Boosted by Beijing’s diplomatic ties and international clout, private companies leverage these state-backed platforms as a springboard for trade by bringing in investment, production capacity, and industry-specific expertise.
The advantages of this approach for Beijing—and the challenge that it poses to foreign companies—are already on full display in Morocco, where years of existing strategic investment, infrastructure development, and geopolitical maneuvering are pushing China closer to vertically integrating EV supply chains, bypassing tariffs, and further reshaping Europe’s auto industry.
It is only in recent years that Morocco has emerged as a key node in China’s EV empire.
For decades, Beijing maintained much closer ties with Morocco’s neighbor and rival, Algeria, but that began to change in the early 2010s as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) took off. In 2016, Morocco joined the growing ranks of countries signing “strategic partnerships” with China, making mutual commitments to expand economic cooperation and recognize each other’s core interests.
The next year, Morocco officially entered the BRI, and China has since poured millions of dollars into Morocco’s energy and transportation sectors. Almost a decade later, that economic relationship has expanded dramatically: In March, China’s committed investment in the country exceeded $10 billion, concentrated mostly in the EV and energy sectors.
China’s EV manufacturing capacity in Morocco builds on years of large-scale, state-backed investment in transportation infrastructure and natural resources. Over the past decade, Chinese SOEs have collaborated on major infrastructure and development projects in Morocco, including bridges, highways, and smart cities. Some of these are directly relevant to the EV industry, such as the chemical processing unit in Khouribga, home to one of the world’s biggest reserves of phosphate, which is critical for EV battery production.
This SOE-led scramble for resources and construction-heavy projects paved the way for private Chinese companies in the EV sector to establish footholds in Morocco and ship to overseas markets. Tanger Tech City, China’s SOE-led flagship collaboration with Morocco, is located less than 30 miles from Tanger Med, the largest container port in Africa. Taking advantage of no-fee business registration and tax-free dividends, private Chinese companies—including the global battery giant BTR New Material Group as well as tire manufacturers Sentury Tire and Guizhou Tyre—have established or announced plans to establish production bases in the industrial zone.
Elsewhere in the country, major private investments include battery manufacturer Gotion’s $1.3 billion factory and a $2 billion joint-venture battery materials factory between China’s CNGR Advanced Material and the Moroccan private equity firm Al Mada.
This isn’t to deny the role of subsidies and preferential financing, which Beijing sees as key tools for supporting companies that are expanding internationally. A 2024 directive, for instance, called on Chinese financial institutions to improve credit approval and lending procedures and to enhance cross-border settlement to “better support companies expanding into international markets”. Closer collaboration among Chinese banks, semi-official trade organizations, and Moroccan banks has also helped to streamline financing and channel investment into the African market.
But these policies are useful to Chinese firms because they are operating in an industrial landscape that SOEs have already shaped, with relatively easy access to necessary resources and infrastructure.
China’s success with this approach has only been possible because it also advances Rabat’s desire to expand domestic manufacturing capability and position Morocco as Africa’s next industrial powerhouse. Chinese investment is expected to generate sorely needed jobs; Morocco’s unemployment rate has hardly dipped below 10 percent for the past decade, and youth unemployment in cities stands at a staggering 47 percent. Officials claim that the Gotion factory alone will create 17,000 local jobs, including 2,300 high-skilled positions.
Beijing has coupled this economic engagement with a subtle diplomatic shift in favor of Rabat’s claims over Western Sahara. For decades, China has avoided explicitly backing either Morocco or Western Sahara, though its rhetoric often leaned toward the latter—and thus to the latter’s main sponsor, Algiers. With one exception in 2018, it consistently voted in favor of United Nations Security Council resolutions extending the peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara and affirming support for the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination.
However, in recent years, China has done an about-face. In 2024, its Ministry of Foreign Affairs implicitly acknowledged the importance of the Western Sahara question for Rabat, stating, “China supports Morocco in maintaining national security and stability and is ready to work with Morocco to continue firmly supporting each other on issues concerning their respective core interests”. Then, last fall, Beijing abstained on the most recent U.N. resolution on the matter, which for the first time endorsed Rabat’s proposal to formally establish Western Sahara as an autonomous region under Moroccan sovereignty.
The full payoff of China’s Moroccan gambit will materialize if and when localized EV manufacturing matures, which could take years. That is still a tall order, as evidenced by the recent shelving of a BYD assembly plant project that had been stalled since 2017 due to budget issues and limited local charging infrastructure, according to a company executive.
Though Chinese automakers are not yet building assembly plants in Morocco, the country matters for everything “upstream” of assembly. It is becoming an integrated ecosystem for the production of batteries, tires, and other components, which reduces Chinese EV companies’ reliance on direct shipments from China and lowers costs for Chinese assembly plants in Europe and Africa.
Morocco also offers Chinese firms convenient access to the European market through the Tanger Med port and—more importantly—a rules-based pathway through Brussels’s tightening trade defenses. Currently, the EU imposes duties of up to 35 percent on EVs manufactured in China. However, vehicles that qualify as Moroccan in origin can enter the European market duty-free. That includes vehicles assembled in Morocco, so long as foreign parts make up less than 45 percent of the finished vehicle’s ex-works price.
In short, if Chinese EV companies succeed in establishing vehicle assembly factories and fully integrating supply chains in Morocco, they will be able to sell vehicles to Europe under a “Made in Morocco” label, avoiding both the 10 percent EU standard automobile tariff and the additional punitive tariff on Chinese-made EVs—reducing the total tariff effect from as much as 45 percent to zero. This would pose an unprecedented threat to what remains one of the EU’s most important industries.
China is rolling out this coordinated approach to overseas industrial policy elsewhere to varying degrees.
In Thailand, for example, China is a key investor in the Eastern Economic Corridor, a flagship regional development initiative anchored by a high-speed railway that will connect several Thai cities and seaports to China. The corridor has, in turn, provided an attractive environment for private Chinese investment. China is now the corridor’s largest source of foreign direct investment, primarily in the EV sector and related industries. Like Tanger Tech City, the corridor offers private Chinese companies major tax incentives and more convenient access to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ market.
The United Arab Emirates offers another example. In 2017, Chinese SOE Jiangsu Provincial Overseas Cooperation and Investment Company Limited (JOCIC) partnered with Abu Dhabi Ports to develop an industrial and special economic zone inside the Khalifa Port’s free trade zone. JOCIC set up a wholly owned UAE subsidiary to manage the park, which lets it attract Chinese private capital while insulating the parent company from project-level and geopolitical risk. The park’s location provides Chinese companies with a convenient base for expansion into the Persian Gulf and wider Middle Eastern markets, along with exemptions from value-added tax and other financial incentives. As of 2025, more than 40 Chinese companies had collectively committed more than $700 million to the park, with a focus on EVs and renewable energy.

articles.title: Singapore climbs 10 places to 8th in global startup ecosystem ranking - Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.summary: Singapore climbs 10 places to 8th in global startup ecosystem ranking  Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.full_text:
At a dinner on Thursday organised by the Action Community for Entrepreneurship Singapore (ACE.SG) to celebrate Singapore’s rise in the global ranking, Manpower Minister and Second Minister for Trade and Industry Tan See Leng said there are now 31 unicorns headquartered here, more than half of which were set up in the past two years.
Highlighting how startups offer disruptive business models and are key to driving economic growth, Dr Tan said they also contribute to Singapore’s “national vision and priorities”.
“Agri-tech startups like Sustenir Group, which uses hydroponics and AI-powered systems to monitor variables like temperature and CO2 levels, support Singapore’s 30 by 30 goal, which is to grow the local agri-food sector’s capability and capacity to sustainably produce 30 per cent of our nutritional needs by 2030,” he said.
ACE.SG, the trade association representing startups in Singapore, recognised the achievements of a number of local startups at the launch of its awards, and signed a memorandum of understanding with the Government Technology Agency during the event.
Under the two-year partnership, they will identify and capitalise on opportunities to raise awareness of ACE.SG programmes as well as GoBusiness – a one-stop platform developed by the Government to provide local businesses with access to government resources and services.
The collaboration also aims to involve startups in GoBusiness’ industry research, user testing, and feedback sessions.
Singapore is currently home to approximately 4,000 tech startups and 200 incubators, and has consistently ranked among the top 10 countries in the Global Innovation Index. It is also among the world’s top 15 countries for ease of source funding, according to Startup Genome.

articles.title: Singapore, Vietnam ink deals to broaden collaboration in green economy, innovation - Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.summary: Singapore, Vietnam ink deals to broaden collaboration in green economy, innovation  Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.full_text:
Singapore and Vietnam have expanded their scope of bilateral economic cooperation and signed new deals on sustainable infrastructure, skills development and the exchange of innovation talent.
Energy connectivity, sustainability, and digital solutions and innovation are new and emerging areas in which both countries want to improve cooperation under the Singapore-Vietnam Connectivity Framework Agreement.
On Monday (28 Aug 2023), they exchanged side letters to mark the expansion of the agreement – the first upgrade since it was signed in 2005 – and also inked three new memorandums of understanding (MOUs) in the areas of green economy, innovation and skills development.
Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, who is on a three-day official visit to the Vietnamese capital of Hanoi, witnessed these events with his counterpart Pham Minh Chinh.
PM Lee had earlier in the day laid a wreath at the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum before attending a welcome ceremony at the Presidential Palace.
He then met Mr Chinh at the Office of the Government.
In a speech at an official dinner hosted by Mr Chinh, PM Lee highlighted the close cooperation between Singapore and Vietnam, and the strong political trust built over the decades.
This year marks 50 years of diplomatic relations between both countries and 10 years of their strategic partnership.
“Through the years, I have watched the Vietnamese leaders work tirelessly alongside their people, who are among the most energetic and talented in Southeast Asia,” said PM Lee.
He added that he was looking forward to meeting young people from Vietnam National University and the Singapore-Vietnam Youth Leaders Exchange Programme on Tuesday.
“We have much to learn from Vietnam, and I hope that this will be a two-way exchange with our youth and professionals,” he said.
On the economic front, Singapore was Vietnam’s second-largest foreign investor as at last December, with a cumulative investment of US$70.8 billion (S$96 billion).
Vietnam was Singapore’s 11th-largest trading partner, with bilateral goods trade growing 16.4 per cent year on year to S$31.3 billion in 2022.

articles.title: CMA CGM, Nike and Gemadept launch a zero-direct-emission electric barge in Vietnam, powered by renewable energy - American Journal of Transportation
articles.summary: CMA CGM, Nike and Gemadept launch a zero-direct-emission electric barge in Vietnam, powered by renewable energy  American Journal of Transportation
articles.full_text:
CMA CGM, Nike and Gemadept have officially launched a new fully electric barge solution in Vietnam, designed to reduce the carbon footprint of inland transportation and contribute to Nike’s supply chain decarbonization efforts.
The 100% electric barge connects Nike’s inland drop-off location in Ho Chi Minh City (formerly Binh Duong province) with Gemalink, Gemadept’s deep-sea terminal in Cai Mep, over a 180-kilometer round trip. Powered by electric batteries and recharged with certified renewable electricity, the barge is expected to avoid approximately 778 tons of CO₂ emissions annually. The integrated solution combines the electric barge, dedicated charging infrastructure and renewable energy production through a solar farm at Gemalink. The barge is designed to transport more than 50,000 TEUs annually, providing a lower-carbon alternative to road transportation for inland cargo movements. The project illustrates the potential of inland waterways to provide more sustainable alternatives for the transportation of goods while improving the environmental performance of supply chains.
Developed by CMA CGM’s New Build and R&D teams, the electric barge incorporates battery technology from CATL and can be recharged in approximately four hours using certified renewable electricity. Its dedicated charging infrastructure at Gemalink is supplied by a solar farm developed at the terminal, creating an integrated solution that combines low-emission transportation with renewable energy production.
The project is designed as a model that can potentially be replicated in other geographies and adapted to other customer supply chains, supporting the broader transition towards more sustainable inland transportation.
Christine Cabau, Executive Vice President Assets and Operations, CMA CGM declared: “Decarbonizing global supply chains requires moving beyond ambition to deliver concrete, scalable solutions. This fully electric barge is a powerful example of what can be achieved when shipping companies, customers and terminal operators combine their expertise and commitment. Together with Nike and Gemadept, we are demonstrating that innovative, lower-carbon inland transportation solutions are already within reach. Now, CMA CGM aims to build on this success to accelerate their deployment across other markets and supply chains.”
Cimarron Nix, Chief Sustainability Officer, NIKE, Inc. declared: “Reducing emissions across a global supply chain takes more than any one company. It takes new ideas, strong partnerships and a willingness to rethink how we operate,” This project with CMA CGM and Gemadept is a great example of how we can work together to turn innovation into practical solutions that reduce our impact while building a more resilient supply chain.”
Do Cong Khanh, Deputy Chief Executive Officer of Gemadept Corporation and Chairman of Gemalink Deep-Sea Port declared: “As a leading port and logistics operator in Vietnam, Gemadept believes that the future of sustainable logistics depends on stronger connections among ports, inland waterways and clean energy. The launch of this fully electric barge with CMA CGM and Nike marks an important milestone in bringing that vision to life. By integrating electric transport, dedicated charging infrastructure and renewable energy at Gemalink, the project demonstrates how partnership and innovation can turn sustainability ambitions into practical solutions. We believe this model has strong potential to be expanded and replicated, contributing to the long-term transition towards low-carbon logistics in Vietnam.”
Supporting Vietnam’s transition towards more sustainable logistics
The project contributes to the development of more sustainable inland transport solutions in Vietnam, while supporting the country’s growing renewable energy and logistics capabilities.
CMA CGM has been present in Vietnam since 2006 and operates five offices in Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, Haiphong, Danang and Quy Nhon, with more than 220 employees. The Group operates 29 weekly mainline services calling at seven ports across the country, connecting Vietnam to major global destinations and supporting its customers through an integrated intermodal network with CEVA Logistics.
The electric barge project further strengthens CMA CGM’s commitment to Vietnam and Southeast Asia and illustrates the Group’s ambition to work with customers and local partners to develop innovative solutions supporting the transition towards more sustainable logistics.

articles.summary: Singapore-Philippines power deals explore cross-border links  Asian Power
articles.full_text:
Agreements also cover advanced nuclear technology and workforce development.
Singapore and the Philippines have agreed to explore cross-border electricity interconnections and deepen cooperation on nuclear energy, as both countries seek to expand regional energy cooperation and diversify their energy options.
Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry Tan See Leng and Philippine Energy Secretary Sharon Garin exchanged Letters of Intent (LOIs) during the opening day of the Singapore International Energy Week (SIEW) Summit 2026.
The interconnection LOI seeks to explore opportunities for cross-border electricity connectivity, which could enable participating countries to trade electricity and make better use of complementary energy resources.
Both sides may engage companies with credible proposals to assess the technical, economic, financial, and commercial aspects of potential interconnections alongside coordination on relevant regulatory approvals and licences.
The LOI also aims to advance the ASEAN Power Grid vision by accelerating efforts to finalise the ASEAN Submarine Power Cable Development Framework.
Under the nuclear LOI, both economies aim to deepen cooperation in advanced nuclear technology, human resource development, the nuclear fuel cycle, nuclear waste management, and civil liability frameworks.
Cooperation includes the exchange of information and expertise amongst government officials and relevant experts, as well as research collaboration.
Both sides also affirmed that nuclear energy cooperation should be pursued safely, securely, and sustainably, consistent with nuclear non-proliferation principles, and applicable international safeguards.
At the SIEW Ministerial Dialogue on regional energy cooperation, Garin emphasised the need for compatible regulations, complementary energy resources, and mutually beneficial arrangements to advance cross-border electricity interconnections.
The Philippines is also exploring electricity links with Malaysia and Indonesia, with bilateral agreements and government coordination seen as key to advancing regional projects.

articles.title: Building Canada-ASEAN Resilience and Accelerating Market Penetration - Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada
articles.summary: Building Canada-ASEAN Resilience and Accelerating Market Penetration  Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada
articles.full_text:
At an economic symposium in Ottawa on October 13, 2026, participants from Canada, Southeast Asia and beyond exchanged views on how Canada and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are building economic resilience and accelerating market penetration. Capitalizing on Southeast Asia’s economic dynamism at the heart of global supply chains and Canada’s resources, innovative technologies, and expertise, bilateral trade grew almost 24 per cent from 2024 to 2025 to $52.5 billion. And yet, practical challenges remain in translating potential into momentum. Participants expressed considerable optimism in the capacity of bilateral and regional free trade agreements to accelerate access to markets and build resilience, reaffirming shared confidence in the rules-based trading system and commitment to international law.
The symposium provided a rich exchange of views on the forthcoming ASEAN Summit in Manila in November, the anticipated conclusion of the ASEAN-Canada Free Trade Agreement (ACAFTA), and the celebration of 50 years of dialogue relations between Canada and ASEAN in 2027. In addition to strategic insights from business leaders, other topics that generated interest were the prospects for Canadian LNG exports to contribute to energy security in Southeast Asia and New Zealand’s approach to economic engagement with ASEAN.
Pooling business, government, diplomatic, and academic perspectives
The symposium, the fourth such event organized by the York Centre for Asian Research’s (YCAR) Canada-ASEAN Initiatives, was hosted by the University of Ottawa’s Telfer Management School, with support from the ASEAN Committee of Ottawa (currently chaired by Indonesia) and the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada. It brought together stakeholders from the Canadian federal government and the diplomatic, business, and academic communities.
Speakers included Global Affairs Canada’s Chief Trade Negotiator for ASEAN, Jay Allen, and Director General for Southeast Asia and Oceania, Alan Bowman. From the Indo-Pacific diplomatic community, speakers included Ambassador Muhsin Syihab of Indonesia, Ambassador of the Philippines Jose Victor Chan-Gonzaga, and New Zealand High Commissioner Wendy Matthews. Senator Clément Gignac, co-chair of the Canada-ASEAN Parliamentary Friendship Group, provided a parliamentary perspective on Canada’s engagement with Southeast Asia.
Strategic business insights were shared by Jean Charest, Honorary Chair of the Canada-ASEAN Business Council, and Motria Savarin-Roy of Sun Life Geostrategic Economics, while think-tank views were provided by Alexandre Veilleux, Senior Program Manager with the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, and Vina Nadjibulla, CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft.
Strategic insights from business leaders
Speakers from the Canada-ASEAN Business Council and Sun Life suggested ways to intensify Canada’s trade with ASEAN, including by investing in long-term partnerships and understanding the diversity of local markets. They also called for closer people-to-people ties between Canada and ASEAN, including in higher education and training, and through the mutual recognition of professional credentials, along the lines of the 2008 Québec-France Agreement. Importantly, the speakers argued, shared recognition of credentials could help reduce regulatory obstacles to professional mobility and help attract talent from ASEAN to Canada, contributing to deeper supply chain integration and co-production of high-value goods and services. At the same time, they argued, business councils and business schools in Canada need to step up their Asia competency game and develop programs targeting deeper engagement with Southeast Asia.
In the face of a sluggish economic growth and low productivity, compounded by persistent trade disruptions inflicted by the current U.S. administration, Canada is moving rapidly in a new direction, actively pursuing closer co-operation with Europe, the Indo-Pacific, and the Middle East. This has led to renewed interest in Canada in exploring new trade architecture and the potential for bloc-to-bloc engagement between the Comprehensive and Progressive Transpacific Partnership (CPTPP) and the European Union. At the same time, Canada needs to consider the fact that the primary trading partner for economies across Southeast Asia is China. Participants noted that Canadians should be asking what Canada’s position is on China’s application to join the CPTPP, and why Canada is not a member of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) linking ASEAN members with China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand.
Canadian companies entering Southeast Asia were advised to invest in building cultural awareness toward long-term trusted relationships and leveraging local expertise and local partnerships. They were also advised to visit the markets often, built trust and establish opportunities together with Southeast Asian partners ahead of the anticipated entry into force of ACAFTA.
International companies have found success in Southeast Asia by collaborating with local partners and adapting their products and services to local demographics, cultures, and lifestyles. For example, partnerships have been important to Sun Life in offering customized insurance products in Malaysia and Shariah-compliant financial services in Indonesia, and to Canadian aviation company CAE in operating a regional training hub in Kuala Lumpur, supported by facilities in four other Southeast Asian countries.
ASEAN, ACAFTA, and the ASEAN Summit in Manila
2027 will mark the 50th anniversary of Canada’s role as an ASEAN dialogue partner, and there was considerable anticipation that the conclusion of ACAFTA would serve as a fitting achievement for that significant milestone. While more than 90 per cent of the text has been agreed, the last 10 per cent includes thorny issues such as market access and rules of origin. The 11 members of ASEAN require government certification regarding the origin of products; in Canada, this determination is made by exporters.
In 2023, the Canada-ASEAN relationship was elevated to a strategic partnership, whose implementation for the next five years is mapped out in the Plan of Action adopted in July 2026. The Plan of Action calls for a “commercially meaningful” ACAFTA that diversifies trade, strengthens supply chain resilience, and expands opportunities for businesses. Implementing the agreement effectively will require closing the awareness gap between Canadian and Southeast Asian companies.
ACAFTA is expected to serve as a foundational agreement for deepening Canada’s entrée into the region. Canada already has trade access to four ASEAN members through the CPTPP: Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, and Vietnam. It aims to have bilateral trade agreements with three more ASEAN economies shortly: the Canada-Indonesia Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) agreed to in 2025, the Canada-Philippines Free Trade Agreement under negotiation, and the Canada-Thailand Free Trade Agreement for which negotiations are about to be launched. ACAFTA will add market access for Canada to three additional ASEAN economies: Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar.
Which sectors will benefit most from ACAFTA’s provisions related to tariffs, non-tariff barriers, and services market access will depend on which companies choose to use the agreement. Ultimately, the intention of free trade agreements – including ACAFTA – is to create a predictable economic and policy environment to ensure that capital and ideas can move freely, regulations are deconflicted, and resilience is strengthened.
Speakers from both the public and private sectors underlined their expectation that trade diversification would continue to be a major Canadian objective in the future, adding they do not expect a decrease in interest in economic engagement with ASEAN, or Asia more broadly, regardless of developments in the U.S. However, they argued that, for Canada to capitalize fully on ACAFTA, it will need to strengthen its domestic east-west trade corridors.
Progress in Canada’s bilateral engagement in Southeast Asia
Within Canada’s Indo-Pacific Strategy, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Indonesia are identified as priorities. The last year has seen high-level progress in engagement with all three. President Prabowo Subianto of Indonesia visited Ottawa in September 2025, witnessing the signing of the Canada-Indonesia CEPA, Canada’s first bilateral trade agreement with an ASEAN member. President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. of the Philippines visited Canada in July 2026, when the bilateral relationship was upgraded to a strategic partnership. Vietnamese President To Lam’s visit to Canada in September this year marked a historic first, and all eight chapters in the Joint Statement on the Strategic Partnership Between Canada and Vietnam arising from that meeting cover areas critical to resilience.
Aspirations for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s anticipated bilateral visit to Manila on the margins of the ASEAN Summit in November include leveraging the recently upgraded relationship to advance co-operation on energy security, trade and investment, economic resilience, and human capital development. The conclusion of negotiations on the Canada Philippines bilateral FTA, along with ACAFTA and the Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), are priority deliverables for Manila’s ASEAN chairmanship this year. Manila also seeks progress on mutual recognition of professional qualifications and credentials, which will require engagement with Canadian provinces.
Prospects for Canadian LNG as a contributor to Southeast Asian energy security
Energy security was discussed at the symposium as an area of shared interest to Canada and ASEAN. | Denis Depoux, global managing director of Roland Berger at the discussion session of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026. Photo: Le Toan | 
According to Depoux, foreign direct investment (FDI) flows are undergoing significant shifts across Asia, driven by three main trends: diversification of production locations, industrial modernisation, and supply chain regionalisation.
Multinational corporations are distributing their manufacturing operations across multiple countries to reduce dependence on a single source of supply. Meanwhile, automation, digitisation and robotics are helping improve productivity and offset the additional costs associated with expanding production networks.
Depoux said that, amid these trends, Vietnam had become a key destination for Chinese and US businesses.
“Companies such as BYD, JOS Solar, and Goldwind are not simply relocating assembly operations to Vietnam, but are also bringing technologies, production processes and innovation capabilities developed across their global networks,” he said.
Vietnam continues to attract investment from US companies such as Apple, Qualcomm and Intel. Although their investment scales vary, US businesses tend to focus on high-value-added sectors such as semiconductors, AI, and advanced technologies.
According to Depoux, the convergence of these investment flows is helping to establish a more deeply integrated manufacturing ecosystem across ASEAN. Notably, this restructuring is reflected not only in changing trade flows but also in the development of tangible manufacturing capabilities.
“For example, LEGO has built its first carbon-neutral factory in Vietnam, with an investment of $1 billion, while maintaining its supplier network in China and integrating the two systems. In this case, it is not China or Vietnam, but China and Vietnam working together,” Depoux said.
This shift is also reflected in Vietnam’s export structure. In 2016, electronics and machinery accounted for around 37 per cent of Vietnam’s exports to the US and Europe. Today, their share has risen to nearly 60 per cent, while the proportions accounted for by apparel and footwear have declined significantly.
However, the development of increasingly complex supply chains is also driving greater demand for financing.
Depoux cited the example of a Vietnamese company that may have to pay for chips and components in Chinese yuan or South Korean won, cover wages in VND, but wait 60-90 days to receive payments in US dollars, euros or Japanese yen.
This creates substantial demand for working capital, foreign exchange services and currency hedging instruments. According to Depoux, this is an area in which financial centres can play a significant role by providing specialised financial services to domestic and foreign-invested enterprises participating in supply chains.
“Vietnam’s economy needs more than capital, as capital alone cannot deliver the 10 per cent growth target,” Depoux said.
Vietnam needs to boost productivity and efficiency, and improve operational performance at every level, from public services and state-owned enterprises to private businesses and foreign-invested enterprises.
This requires innovation and the modernisation of industrial supply chains. Economists refer to this as total factor productivity. It is essential to offset the declining returns on capital while helping businesses minimise the additional costs incurred when scaling up production capacity.
Vietnam therefore needs to move from assembly towards advanced manufacturing, while undertaking extensive digitisation of logistics operations, from seaports to factories. This process cannot rely on short-term capital flows or one-off investments. Instead, it requires substantial, long-term and patient capital to improve operational efficiency over a period of many years.
Depoux pointed out that Vietnam’s credit-to-GDP ratio had reached around 146 per cent, indicating that the banking system was shouldering a substantial share of the economy’s financing needs. Meanwhile, public debt stood at around 35 per cent of GDP, leaving some fiscal headroom to mobilise resources for development investment.
“Vietnam’s problem is not an excessive public debt burden, but a banking system carrying too much credit exposure while the economy lacks sufficient long-term capital,” he said.
Another paradox highlighted by Depoux is the divergence between foreign direct investment and foreign portfolio investment. While foreign investment in Vietnamese factories has reached high levels, foreign investors were net sellers of nearly $5 billion worth of Vietnamese shares last year.
“Capital flowing into factories favours and trusts Vietnam, but capital in the financial markets still needs an additional boost,” he added.
FTSE Russell’s upgrade of Vietnam’s market is a first step. Vietnam needs to continue working towards being classified as an emerging market by Morgan Stanley Capital International, while also securing an investment-grade sovereign credit rating.
These are important conditions for attracting pension funds, institutional investment funds and other investors capable of providing stable, long-term capital.
Depoux recommended prioritising the development of the corporate capital market.
“Vietnam’s corporate bond market currently accounts for around 10–11 per cent of GDP, having previously peaked at 18 per cent, while the government’s target is 20 per cent. Vietnam needs to develop a larger, deeper and more liquid corporate bond market to finance industrial modernisation,” he said.
He also proposed making the achievement of an investment-grade credit rating a national objective. “As I mentioned, this is fundamental to attracting investment,” he said.
In addition, Vietnam needs to accelerate industrial modernisation, strengthen domestic and international infrastructure connectivity, and leverage the convergence of the physical economy and the digital economy to pull in technology capital.
At the same time, Ho Chi Minh City and Danang should be positioned as resilient supply chain finance centres. The focus should be on serving supply chains that integrate physical manufacturing with technology, thereby meeting their growing financing needs.
