articles.title: Singapore’s digital trade tops S$520 billion, outpacing overall trade growth: SingStat estimates - 联合早报
articles.summary: Singapore’s digital trade tops S$520 billion, outpacing overall trade growth: SingStat estimates  联合早报
articles.full_text:
Amid growing digitalisation, Singapore’s digital trade rose from S$372 billion in 2021 to S$521.1 billion in 2024, recording a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 11.9%, well ahead of the 7.4% growth in overall trade over the same period.
The latest experimental estimates released by the Singapore Department of Statistics (SingStat) show that digital trade’s share of Singapore’s overall trade rose steadily from 19.2% in 2021 to 21.7% in 2024. Over the same period, the ratio of digital trade to gross domestic product (GDP) increased from 62.8% to 68.1%, reflecting the increasingly significant role of digitalisation in driving Singapore’s economy.
Digital trade is a component of international trade in goods and services, covering exports and imports of goods and services that are digitally ordered or delivered.
Digital trade in goods and services is classified according to how they are ordered and delivered. Singapore’s digital trade estimates are compiled mainly from trade and industry surveys, supplemented by other sources such as credit card transactions and household surveys.
Digitally delivered or ordered services, such as cloud services and streaming platform services, make up the bulk of Singapore’s digital trade.
In 2024, trade in these services reached S$439.8 billion, accounting for more than 80% of the total, with a four-year CAGR of 12.5%.
By comparison, goods ordered through e-commerce or digital platforms totalled S$81.3 billion in 2024, with a four-year CAGR of 8.8%.
Digital trade exports grew from S$231.9 billion in 2021 to S$307.2 billion in 2024, a CAGR of 9.8%. Services accounted for S$250.6 billion of these exports.
Digital trade imports grew even faster, rising from S$140.1 billion in 2021 to S$213.9 billion in 2024, a CAGR of 15.1%. Notably, surging demand from consumers and businesses ordering physical goods on cross-border e-commerce platforms drove imports of digitally ordered goods to nearly double, from S$12.7 billion to S$24.7 billion, a CAGR of 25.0%.
International comparisons based on 2023 data show that digital trade accounted for 20.9% of Singapore’s total trade. This was higher than in economies such as Canada (14.8%), Greece (14.5%), Italy (14.2%) and Norway (10.2%), but below the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) average of 25.9%. Singapore also trailed leading countries such as the UK (55.2%) and Sweden (43.6%).
SingStat’s analysis noted how this indicates that Singapore still has considerable room for growth in deepening digital adoption and expanding digital trade.
Beyond cross-border trade flows, the first experimental estimates for the Digital Economy Satellite Account, released at the same time by SingStat, show that local digital industries also provide strong support for the real economy. In 2023, Singapore’s digital industries generated S$152.7 billion in gross value added, accounting for 23.7% of the national total and maintaining a substantial contribution of more than 20% of GDP.
SingStat said the experimental framework, developed using OECD standards, would give policymakers and businesses clearer, more comparable data for assessing Singapore’s position in international value chains and the digital economy.
Maisie Chong, Standard Chartered’s head of trade and working capital for ASEAN and South Asia, told Lianhe Zaobao (LHZB): “Singapore has significant structural strengths in connectivity, services and digital infrastructure, so our baseline expectation is that its digital trade will continue to grow faster than overall trade in 2025 and 2026. However, with a more volatile external environment, growth may normalise from the exceptional double-digit rates seen in the early phase of accelerated digitalisation.”
Chong said a Standard Chartered study, the Future of Trade report, further supported this trend. Between 2016 and 2025, global exports of digitally delivered services grew by 136%, compared with 70% growth in total exports of goods and services.
The study found that recent demand for computer services, artificial intelligence, cloud delivery, cyber security and broader digital transformation had supported this growth momentum.
She noted that these trends remained favourable for a highly connected, services-oriented economy such as Singapore, even amid a more volatile external trade environment.

articles.title: China+1 is Not Enough: Why India and ASEAN Need a Shared Production Strategy - India Narrative
articles.summary: China+1 is Not Enough: Why India and ASEAN Need a Shared Production Strategy  India Narrative
articles.full_text:
The changing landscape of global industry presents major opportunities for India and ASEAN. US–China trade tensions, rising geopolitical risks, and the need for multinational companies to diversify their supply chains have driven the China+1 strategy. Companies are not necessarily leaving China, but are beginning to locate part of their production capacity in other countries to reduce dependence on a single location.
However, a fundamental problem remains: industrial relocation does not automatically create regional economic integration. India and ASEAN countries may both attract investment but still fail to build complementary production ecosystems. If each country offers only tax incentives, subsidies, and competitive wages to compete for the same investors, the result could be a subsidy race rather than an improvement in regional competitiveness. Therefore, the China+1 strategy needs to evolve into a shared India–ASEAN production strategy.
ASEAN–India economic relations have developed through their dialogue partnership since 1995 and the ASEAN–India Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA), which was signed in 2009 and entered into force in 2010. In 2025, both sides continued reviewing AITIGA to make the agreement more effective and responsive to changes in global trade.
This development continued in 2026. At the ASEAN–India Economic Ministers’ Consultation in Manila in September, both sides discussed trade, investment, and the revision of AITIGA. Bilateral trade in goods reached US$128.38 billion in India’s 2025–2026 fiscal year, while ASEAN accounted for approximately 10.55% of India’s total global trade. These figures demonstrate that the relationship has a significant economic foundation, rather than being based solely on diplomatic proximity.
Nevertheless, substantial trade does not guarantee an integrated division of production roles. The next challenge is to ensure that investment, technology, components, skilled labour, and markets from both regions are interconnected.
Industrial Relocation
Investment data show that supply chain transformation is not merely a talking point. According to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025, foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows into ASEAN increased by 8% to US$226 billion in 2024, while global FDI flows declined by 11%. ASEAN’s manufacturing investment surged by nearly 150% to US$44 billion. Electronics, electric vehicles, pharmaceuticals, and the digital economy have become important parts of this transformation.
Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia offer different production capabilities. Vietnam is developing as an electronics manufacturing base; Thailand has an automotive ecosystem; Malaysia has strengths in semiconductors and electronics; while Indonesia possesses critical mineral resources for batteries and electric vehicles.
India is also making progress. According to the Indian Ministry of Commerce, its electronics production increased from ₹1.9 trillion in 2014–2015 to ₹11.3 trillion in 2024–2025. Electronics exports rose to ₹3.27 trillion over the same period. Mobile phone production and manufacturing incentive policies have been part of this transformation.
However, these figures must be interpreted carefully. Increased investment in India and ASEAN does not entirely represent direct relocation from China. Some of it reflects new capacity expansion, investment to serve domestic markets, or diversification that retains production facilities in China. Thus, China+1 is not a simple transfer of industry but the formation of a more geographically distributed production network.
Why India and ASEAN Need to Cooperate
The theory of comparative advantage explains that countries benefit when they specialise according to their relative capabilities and costs. However, in the modern economy, advantage is no longer determined solely by final products. Countries also compete through their positions in global value chains.
A study by the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia (ERIA) shows that ASEAN has relatively strong connections to global production networks, while India’s integration into global value chains still has room for improvement. The study highlights the importance of cross-regional investment and identifying manufacturing complementarities.
From the perspective of regional production network theory, economic benefits are greater when companies can combine the advantages of different locations. India has a large domestic market, technological capabilities, and a broad industrial and labour base. ASEAN offers supplier networks, ports, industrial zones, export experience, and access to various markets across East Asia and the Pacific.
If both sides operate independently, they risk duplicating investments and competing in the same products. Conversely, if they are connected, components can be produced in one country, processed in another, assembled at the most efficient location, and marketed through regional trade networks. This is the difference between merely attracting investment and building collective competitiveness.
Building a Shared Production Strategy
First, India and ASEAN need to develop a cross-regional supply chain map. This mapping should identify priority industries, missing suppliers, technological requirements, and the most competitive production stages in each country. Electronics, semiconductors, electric vehicle batteries, pharmaceuticals, and industrial machinery are suitable starting sectors.
Second, the revision of AITIGA should be directed towards facilitating trade in intermediate goods and components. Simplifying rules of origin, customs procedures, technical standards, and certification would help companies distribute production processes across borders without facing excessive administrative costs.
Third, investment cooperation must go beyond individual countries’ investment promotion efforts. Governments can establish regional supplier forums that bring together multinational companies, local industries, financial institutions, and research centres. The objective is not merely to attract factories but to strengthen the capacity of local companies to become part of international supply chains.
India needs to strengthen manufacturing competitiveness, improve regulatory certainty, create opportunities for technology partnerships, and leverage its domestic market to achieve production scale. India can also serve as a centre for design, engineering, industrial software, and the production of selected components.
ASEAN needs to strengthen connectivity among its member states, harmonise standards, and connect industrial zones and ports with Indian supplier networks. Indonesia can contribute through critical minerals, battery materials, and downstream industrial development. Malaysia can strengthen semiconductors and electronics, Thailand automotive manufacturing, and Vietnam electronics manufacturing and export networks.
ASEAN itself is not a uniform economy. Therefore, the division of roles should be based on each country’s capabilities rather than rigid political quotas. India and ASEAN must also involve the private sector as the main driver, while governments ensure fair competition and that investment benefits reach workers and local industries.
From Competition to Complementarity
China+1 offers an opportunity, but that opportunity will not endure through investment incentives alone. Companies will choose locations that offer productivity, policy certainty, quality suppliers, infrastructure, and market access. India and ASEAN do not need to build a production bloc that is closed to China. Instead, they should build a more resilient, open, and diversified network, giving companies more options without sacrificing efficiency.
Ultimately, the measure of success is not how many factories have been moved out of China. It is how far India and ASEAN can improve value addition, productivity, job quality, technology transfer, and industrial competitiveness.
China+1 should be a starting point, not the final destination. If India and ASEAN can transform investment competition into a shared production strategy, they will not only become alternatives to China but also establish one of the most important manufacturing centres in the Indo-Pacific economy.

articles.title: Expert Roland Berger offers advice on mobilizing capital for Vietnam's growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Expert Roland Berger offers advice on mobilizing capital for Vietnam's growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On the afternoon of October 28th, during the in-depth discussion session on the theme "Identifying New Growth Drivers" within the framework of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026, Mr. Denis Depoux, Global Managing Director of Roland Berger, analyzed the movements of global supply chains and the requirements placed on the Vietnamese financial market. 
|  | 
| Denis Depoux, Global CEO of Roland Berger . Photo: Le Toan. | 
 Vietnam in the wave of Asian supply chain restructuring
 According to Denis Depoux's analysis, FDI flows are shifting strongly in Asia, stemming from three main trends: diversification of production locations, industrial modernization, and regionalization of supply chains.
 Multinational corporations are diversifying their manufacturing operations across multiple countries to reduce reliance on a single supply source. Simultaneously, automation, digitalization, and robotics are improving productivity and offsetting the costs incurred from expanding production networks.
 Denis Depoux stated that, in this trend, Vietnam is becoming an important destination for Chinese and American businesses.
 Corporations like BYD, JOS Solar, Goldwind, and Gotion are not simply moving their assembly operations to Vietnam, but are also bringing in technologies, production processes, and innovative capabilities developed within their global networks.
 Vietnam continues to attract investment from American companies such as Apple , Qualcomm, and Intel. While the scale of investment varies, American companies tend to focus on high value-added sectors such as semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and advanced technologies.
 According to expert Roland Berger, the convergence of these capital flows is contributing to the formation of a more deeply interconnected production ecosystem in ASEAN. Notably, this restructuring process is not only reflected in changes in trade flows, but is also linked to the development of substantial production capacity.
 For example, LEGO built its first carbon neutrality plant in Vietnam with an investment of $1 billion, while maintaining its supplier network in China and integrating the two systems. “In this case, it’s not China or Vietnam, but China and Vietnam working together,” Denis Depoux emphasized.
 This shift is also reflected in the export structure. In 2016, electronics and machinery accounted for approximately 37% of Vietnam's exports to the US and Europe. Currently, this proportion has risen to nearly 60%, while the share of the garment and footwear industries has decreased significantly.
 However, the development of complex supply chains also brings with it increasingly large financial needs.
 Denis Depoux gave an example: a Vietnamese business might have to pay for chips and components in Chinese yuan or South Korean won, pay salaries in Vietnamese dong, but only receive payment in USD, euros, or Japanese yen after 60-90 days.
 This creates a significant demand for working capital, foreign exchange services, and exchange rate risk hedging tools. According to him, this is one area where financial centers can play a crucial role, by providing specialized financial services to domestic businesses and FDI enterprises participating in the supply chain.
 Long-term capital gap and productivity enhancement requirements.
 "The Vietnamese economy needs more than just capital, because capital alone cannot achieve the 10% growth target," Denis Depoux stated .
 According to expert Roland Berger, Vietnam needs to improve productivity, efficiency, and operational effectiveness at all levels, from public services and state-owned enterprises to private and foreign-invested enterprises.
 This requires innovation and modernization of the industrial chain. Economists call this total factor productivity. This is essential to effectively offset the declining return on capital, while also helping businesses minimize costs incurred when scaling up production capacity.
 Therefore, Vietnam needs to shift from assembly to advanced manufacturing, while simultaneously digitizing its logistics operations extensively, from seaports to factories. This process cannot rely on short-term capital or one-time investments, but requires long-term, large-scale capital and patience to improve operational efficiency over many years.
 Regarding the ability to mobilize capital, Denis Depoux pointed out that the credit-to-GDP ratio has reached approximately 146%, indicating that the banking system is handling a very large volume of capital financing for the economy. Meanwhile, public debt is only at about 35% of GDP, creating considerable room to mobilize resources for development investment.
 "Vietnam's problem is not the excessive burden of public debt, but rather that the banking system is carrying too much credit, while the economy has not been provided with enough long-term capital," he said.
 Another paradox mentioned by Denis Depoux is the difference between foreign direct and indirect investment flows. While foreign investment in factories in Vietnam reached high levels, foreign investors sold a net of nearly $5 billion worth of Vietnamese stocks last year.
 "Investment capital flows into factories that favor and trust Vietnam, but capital flows in the financial market still need a boost," he added.
 According to him, FTSE's upgrade of the market is the first step. Vietnam needs to continue working towards the goal of being classified as an emerging market by MSCI, while also achieving an investment-grade national credit rating.
 These are crucial conditions for attracting pension funds, institutional investment funds, and investors capable of providing a stable source of capital over the long term.
 The fundamental factor in attracting investment capital.
 Based on the above analysis, expert Roland Berger recommends prioritizing the development of the corporate capital market. Currently, the size of this market in Vietnam is equivalent to 10-11% of GDP, having peaked at 18% in the past, while the government 's target is 20%. Vietnam needs to aim for a large-scale, deep, and highly liquid corporate bond market to finance the process of industrial modernization.
 He also suggested that Vietnam consider achieving an investment credit rating as a national goal. "As I mentioned, this is a fundamental factor in attracting investment," he said.
 In addition, Vietnam needs to promote industrial modernization, strengthen domestic and international infrastructure connectivity, and leverage the convergence of physical production and the digital economy to attract technology investment.
 At the same time, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang need to be positioned as highly resilient supply chain finance centers. The focus should be on serving supply chains that combine physical manufacturing and technology, thereby meeting the growing financial needs of these supply chains.

The first 10 members of the Vietnam International Financial Center in Ho Chi Minh City (VIFC-HCMC) plan to mobilize and invest about $2.7 billion by 2027 in projects spanning infrastructure, education, energy, and technology.
The members were announced on Wednesday at the Autumn Economic Forum 2026, in the presence of Prime Minister Le Minh Hung, government officials, and HCMC leaders
The 10 founding members are EQuest Capital Co., Ltd.; Son Kim Capital IFC Co., Ltd.; VinaCapital International Partners Co., Ltd.; Saigon Marina IFC Co., Ltd.; Gemadept Holdings Maritime Investment and Development Co., Ltd.; Rovela Pay One-Member Co., Ltd.; REE Energy Finance Co., Ltd.; Vietnam IFC Commodity Exchange JSC; AG&P Holding Vietnam Co., Ltd.; and Keppel Asset Management (Vietnam).
All 10 members are holding companies whose primary role is to hold and manage equity stakes or capital contributions in other businesses.
The holding companies have a combined registered charter capital and committed contributions of $33.63 million. Their planned investments through 2027 will target education, infrastructure, maritime services, logistics, energy, financial technology, payment solutions, and commodity trading infrastructure.
Several members have outlined major fundraising and investment plans. Saigon Marina IFC has committed to raise about $816 million to develop technology and physical infrastructure for the VIFC-HCMC ecosystem.
AG&P Holding Vietnam plans to raise and invest about $425 million across the liquefied natural gas (LNG), power, and data center value chains. EQuest Capital has committed to mobilizing about $325 million under a cooperation agreement with Standard Chartered Bank’s New York branch to develop education infrastructure in Vietnam, with a focus on the Southwestern HCMC University Urban Area.
Son Kim Capital IFC plans to raise about $275 million for infrastructure development within VIFC-HCMC, while REE Energy Finance has committed to mobilizing about $200 million for renewable energy projects.
Keppel Asset Management (Vietnam) is also exploring the formation of co-investment platforms with global partners to raise up to $1 billion, mainly from third-party investors. The funds would target opportunities in infrastructure, real estate, trade, and services within VIFC-HCMC.
VIFC-HCMC said the investment plans marked a shift from establishing a membership ecosystem to connecting capital with specific projects. The center is continuing to develop its licensing framework to attract specialized financial institutions, initially focusing on investment funds and asset management. It expects to finalize and issue procedures and regulations for admitting investment funds in November 2026.
Banks, securities firms, and other businesses subject to specific licensing requirements will be considered in phases as the relevant regulations are introduced.

articles.title: Vietnam can’t win high-tech investment on land alone: 2026 Autumn Economic Forum - Thông tấn xã Việt Nam
articles.summary: Vietnam can’t win high-tech investment on land alone: 2026 Autumn Economic Forum  Thông tấn xã Việt Nam
articles.full_text:
Land alone can’t attract tech projects
Vietnam has a major opportunity in the global digital shift as AI, cloud computing and digital services increasingly shape economic activity. Capturing it requires planning infrastructure as a whole rather than project by project, Bill Giannikos, Director of the Global Services Centre and Data Centre at Aurecon Vietnam, told the CEO 500 programme, themed “The Convergence of FDI, Technology and Global Financial Flows,” at the 2026 Autumn Economic Forum on October 26.
According to him, data centre development has to be planned alongside land, power, telecoms and supporting services. Investors need clear information on land availability, power capacity, supply timelines and connectivity before committing to large projects.
Giannikos pointed to Australia’s Victoria state, which coordinates land, energy and connectivity planning to build its digital ecosystem. He proposed that Vietnam, particularly Ho Chi Minh City, study creating dedicated zones for digital infrastructure, with essential requirements built into planning from the start.
Beyond infrastructure, he stressed linking computing capacity with universities, enterprises and the workforce to speed up AI adoption in manufacturing, logistics, health care, education and public services. Returns on investment therefore depend not only on data centre capacity, but on how the technology is adopted and the value it creates for the economy.
Infrastructure must also scale up and adapt to new technologies while taking into account energy and water efficiency and long-term resilience. That demands coordination among authorities, utilities, operators and technology suppliers from the planning stage.
Nguyen The Duy, Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors and Deputy CEO of Becamex Group, said the larger development space after the merger gives Ho Chi Minh City a chance to build high-tech industrial hubs and modern urban areas.
According to Duy, a new generation of FDI investors is looking beyond land and factory space, paying attention also to connectivity infrastructure, technology access, workforce and an ecosystem of production support services. Becamex is developing next-generation industrial parks that are smart, eco-friendly and sustainable, linking production infrastructure with research, technology transfer, automation and workforce training.
Notably, Becamex aims to develop a science and technology urban area in northern Ho Chi Minh City into an integrated ecosystem of high-tech industry, research and development, innovation, training and modern urban living. The area is planned to connect to the city downtown via expressways, railways, metro lines and regional logistics networks.
To realise this vision, its representative proposed that the city continue building breakthrough mechanisms to foster an industrial and sci-tech ecosystem capable of attracting high-added-value FDI projects.
Clearing bottlenecks so technology adds value
Jesse Choi, General Director of Sunwah Southeast Asia, suggested that the city create conditions for firms to test technological solutions in real-world environments. The city could support pilot sites, develop technical standards and risk management mechanisms, and set out a roadmap for bringing qualified technologies into commercial application, he said.
Citing the AI use to optimise wastewater treatment as an example, Choi said the solution could cut operating costs by about 20–25%. Technologies such as drones and self-driving electric vehicles also have potential for use in logistics and urban services.
San Eng, Chairman of the Singapore-based WorkOptional.ai, said beyond data centres and computing power, the market is seeing growing demand for services that support AI agents capable of performing work in place of humans. This trend is driving demand for communication, transaction, payment, identity, authentication and risk management systems. These could become important components of digital economy infrastructure in the next phase.
He also said Vietnam has advantages in absorbing technology from many markets, developing domestic digital platforms and pooling a workforce capable of adapting to new technologies. In his view, the city should study developing infrastructure for an AI-agent economy, while tightening links between its Vietnam International Financial Centre and investors and technology companies.
Working sessions with partners in Vietnam before the 2027 first quarter to seek cooperation opportunities and develop technology and financial platforms in line with the AI economy trend are also needed, he said./.

articles.title: Revolut's expanded Singapore office and S$350 million investment - Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.summary: Revolut's expanded Singapore office and S$350 million investment  Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.full_text:
This press release was issued by Revolut.
Revolut, the global financial leader serving more than 80 million retail customers and 850,000 business customers worldwide, today announced plans for a new Singapore office at Collyer Quay Centre. The move underscores Revolut’s long-term commitment to the market, as it celebrates seven years since launching in Singapore. It also forms part of Revolut’s plans to invest nearly S$350 million in Singapore over the next five years, spanning product innovation, business growth and the expansion of its local workforce.
A new home in the heart of Singapore’s financial district
The company has signed a five-year lease for approximately 8,880 sq ft of office space on the 9th floor of Collyer Quay Centre and the new office is scheduled to open in early 2027.
Located along Collyer Quay, the new office will place Revolut at the heart of Singapore’s financial district, providing a central base to deepen relationships with customers, businesses and partners while supporting the company’s continued growth in the market. The new space will support Revolut’s growing Singapore team as the company scales its local workforce to more than 300 employees over the next three years. Revolut nearly doubled its Singapore workforce in 2025, with headcount increasing by more than 95% year-on-year, and is hiring for roles across engineering, product, data and AI.
Designed as a flexible space, the office will support collaboration, team gatherings, customer and partner engagement, and events, while maintaining flexibility in how and where employees work. Revolut’s presence will extend beyond the office itself, with two Revolut logos prominently displayed on the building’s facade — one facing Marina Bay and the other facing the Esplanade — giving the company a distinctive presence in SIngapore’s iconic skyline.
Nearly S$350 million to accelerate growth and innovation
The new office forms part of Revolut’s broader commitment to invest nearly S$350 million in Singapore over the next five years, spanning product innovation, business growth and the expansion of its local workforce.
The investment reflects Revolut’s confidence in Singapore following its second consecutive year of net profitability in the market in 2025, alongside strong growth across its business.
The commitment will support continued investment in Revolut’s products, technology and people in Singapore, as the company enters its next phase of growth. Singapore will also continue to serve as an important base for Revolut’s expansion across Southeast Asia, supporting the development of products, partnerships and local expertise as the company grows its presence across the region.
From travel product to everyday financial platform
Since launching in Singapore in 2019, Revolut has evolved from a product best known for travel into a broader financial platform for everyday spending and financial management.
In 2025, domestic transaction volumes grew by more than 30% year-on-year, with domestic transactions now accounting for nearly half of total activity. Peer-to-peer payment volumes increased by close to 40%, while both the number and volume of virtual card payments grew by more than 55%. Meanwhile, the number of customers using Wealth & Trading increased by close to 55%.
Revolut continues to expand its offering in Singapore, with recent developments including the launch of Ultra, enhanced paid plans with new partner benefits from brands including foodpanda and OpenAI, and expanded multi-currency capabilities including CNY and VND.
Together, these developments reflect the company’s evolution from a travel-focused product into an increasingly comprehensive platform for everyday financial needs.
Building a platform for ambitious businesses
Revolut’s growth in Singapore extends beyond its retail offering. Its business customer base grew fivefold in 2025, reflecting increasing demand from companies looking for more integrated ways to manage payments, cash and day-to-day financial operations.
Globally, Revolut Business has surpassed US$1 billion in annualised revenue, reflecting the scale of its B2B offering. In Singapore, Revolut Business continues to see robust growth. Over the past year (Aug 2025 vs Aug 2026), deposit balances and transfer volumes each increased threefold, while card payment volumes increased tenfold.
Over the past year, Revolut has expanded its Business offering in Singapore with launches including Flexible Cash Funds and a full suite of merchant acquiring solutions, bringing account-to-account, online and in-person payments together within a core business account.
These capabilities give businesses a more integrated way to manage their finances, from making and receiving payments to managing cash and accessing financial tools within a single platform.

articles.title: How Singapore’s robust ecosystem supported EDPR’s regional venture into solar innovations - Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.summary: How Singapore’s robust ecosystem supported EDPR’s regional venture into solar innovations  Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.full_text:
Along the Straits of Johor between Singapore and Malaysia is an unusual sight – a nearshore floating solar photovoltaic system of over 13,000 solar panels. One of the world’s largest floating solar farms on seawater, the project is an innovative solution specially designed by EDP Renewables APAC for land-scarce, densely populated cities like Singapore to tap into renewable energy. The successful installation of the five megawatt-peak (MWp) project, which can generate enough solar energy to power 1,100 four-room flats in Singapore per year, paves the way for more of such projects to follow in the region.
Renewable energy from nearshore floating solar farms and other innovative sources are crucial to accelerating Southeast Asia’s energy transition. A joint report by EDB and McKinsey & Company estimates that solar and onshore wind power generation will have to increase between seven and twelvefold to meet the net-zero emission targets set by countries in the region. This in turn is a growth opportunity for businesses – according to a study by the International Energy Agency (IEA), clean energy investment needs to increase by nearly five-fold to about US$190 billion (S$260 billion) by 2035 in order to hit regional net-zero goals1.
Recognising this potential for growth, global renewable energy leader EDPR established its Asia Pacific headquarters in Singapore via the acquisition of local renewable energy company Sunseap in February 20222.
Since then, EDP Renewables APAC has grown into a true regional trailblazer for renewables deployment, with a committed capacity of 1.6 gigawatt-peak (GWp) of solar energy projects (as of December 2024) in the region. The company has also more than tripled its total renewables capacity since February 2022, surpassing the one GW milestone. We examine some key decisions that played a major role in their success.
Prioritising scale and commitment when selecting a regional headquarters location
According to a report by Bain, Temasek, and Amazon Web Services, strong public-private partnerships are key to the success of any renewable energy deployment. Clear government objectives that set the pace of climate action and investment also provide a conducive environment for private sector investments, which can facilitate scalable energy solutions for the region.
To this end, Singapore stands out as a natural choice for renewable energy companies such as EDPR. Take the Singapore Green Plan 2030, a whole-of-nation movement to advance Singapore’s national agenda on sustainable development. Among its 2030 targets is to increase solar deployment to at least two GWp — driving demand for renewable energy companies like EDPR.

articles.title: MAS Tells Banks to Scrutinise Clients Linked to Haze - Fintech Singapore
articles.summary: MAS Tells Banks to Scrutinise Clients Linked to Haze  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has reinforced its expectations for banks to manage environmental risks linked to haze, including limiting financing or ending customer relationships where environmental laws have been clearly breached.
MAS said banks should identify, assess, manage and monitor material environmental risks arising from their activities and exposures, including pollution and deforestation.
Banks should also consider relevant information released by the National Environment Agency (NEA) under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (THPA).
Banks expected to assess customers linked to haze
MAS expects banks to engage customers potentially linked to activities contributing to haze and obtain sufficient information about their involvement.
This includes assessing whether customers have adequate measures to prevent, detect and stop fires.
Where banks identify heightened environmental risks, they should take steps to address them. These may include imposing conditions, reviewing financing terms, limiting further exposures or reassessing customer relationships.
Clear breaches of environmental laws would warrant stronger measures, including limiting exposures or ending customer relationships, according to MAS.
MAS reinforces existing environmental risk guidelines
The regulator also expressed support for the stance taken by Singapore’s three local banks, DBS, OCBC and UOB, against burning practices.
These expectations are covered under MAS’ Guidelines on Environmental Risk Management, issued in 2020, and further elaborated in its Guidelines on Transition Planning, issued in March 2026.
The transition planning guidelines will take effect in September 2027, following an 18-month transition period.
MAS said it has reinforced its existing supervisory expectations with banks in response to the current haze situation.

articles.title: More Women, Skilled Workers Needed for Southeast Asia’s Energy Transition - Cambodianess
articles.summary: More Women, Skilled Workers Needed for Southeast Asia’s Energy Transition  Cambodianess
articles.full_text:
- 
                                    By:
                                    
                                    
                                
- Sao Phal Niseiy
- October 29, 2026, 2:15 PM
SINGAPORE – Experts have called for greater investment in skilled workers and more women in the renewable energy workforce to speed up Southeast Asia’s energy transition and advance electrification.
Lin Yang, deputy executive secretary for programme at the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP), said many countries in the region have ambitious energy transition plans, but a shortage of skilled workers is slowing progress.
“These people include planners, engineers, technicians, regulators as well as system operators who can manage integrated cross-border systems,” Lin said at Singapore International Energy Week (SIEW).
She also highlighted gender disparities in the workforce. But the energy transition needs to go hand in hand with gender equality as the global energy system reaches a critical juncture.
“We also need to bring more women into the workforce. Women’s labor force participation in the region is only 44 percent against 76 percent for men,” she said. "We need to connect workers working in carbon-intensive industries to re-skilling and new opportunities."
The disparity is evident worldwide, with women underrepresented in the energy sector, according to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) 2025 World Energy Employment report. Women account for only 32 percent of full-time jobs in renewable energy. In ASEAN, women make up just 8 percent of the energy workforce, according to estimates by the ASEAN Climate Change and Energy Project (ACCEPT).
Razib Dawood, executive director of the ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE), agreed that Southeast Asia needs more skilled workers who can adapt to the changing demands of the energy sector, particularly as countries push for electrification.
“We have to have ready graduates or engineers or scientists for the expanded infrastructure, so you have to get ready, but again, this is a good time to address employment,” Razib told Cambodianess, adding that universities need to align their training with the needs of the energy sector.
He cited the growing use of electric vehicles, which requires mechanics trained to repair batteries, and the need for engineers capable of operating nuclear power plants
“Training them today so that we will have people to operate the nuclear plants. This is a new technology, and also wind power, where you need people who know about anti-rusting and so on,” he said.
A workforce with the right skills and experience will be critical to operating and maintaining future energy infrastructure.
“That is why we need that for the transition. It’s an opportunity,” he said.
Demand for nuclear expertise is also expected to rise. Speaking at the SIEW summit this week, IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said interest in nuclear power is growing.
“Three and a half years ago, I claimed nuclear is making a comeback. The historic number is now 90 gigawatts of nuclear power plants under construction. This is the highest in the last four decades,” he said.
Connectivity 2.0: Building Connected Systems
Lin said globalisation and multilateralism are under strain, making it important for Asia and the Pacific to pioneer a new model of cooperation that builds confidence, advances the clean energy transition and promotes shared prosperity across the region.
She cited two lessons from UNESCAP’s 80-year history. The first is strategic investment in physical connectivity, including roads, railways, ports and power infrastructure. The second is a development philosophy centred on people, with economic growth accompanied by wider access to education, health care and decent work.
“The dividends were widely shared,” she said.
Long-term cooperation, she explained, requires both well-connected systems and strong human capital. Those lessons are increasingly relevant as trade frictions, geopolitical tensions, climate disasters and supply chain restructuring create new vulnerabilities.
“Energy systems feel the pressures because many economies remain highly dependent on particular fuels, technologies, or routes,” Lin said, noting that these pressures reflect structural changes rather than temporary disruptions.
She said the region needs to develop “Connectivity 2.0,” moving beyond connecting places to integrating physical, digital, financial and institutional systems.
“That’s what we call Connectivity 2.0. which can reinforce one another. We need integrated corridors, for example, trade corridors, transport corridors, digital corridors, maybe computing corridors and energy corridors, how they can be integrated and planned together,” she said.
Power connectivity is central to this shift, she explained, adding that green power corridors are not simply transmission lines carrying renewable electricity from one country to another. They can also serve as corridors for development.
“They can unlock renewable resources, allowing countries to share flexibility and reserves, reduce exposure to fuel shocks, and create investments, industry and jobs,” she said.
“Artificial intelligence and the data centers are a stress test for this model.”

articles.title: International capital raising: a missing link in Vietnam’s double-digit growth ambitions - Theinvestor
articles.summary: International capital raising: a missing link in Vietnam’s double-digit growth ambitions  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam needs to diversify its funding sources and reduce its reliance on bank lending to achieve its target of average annual GDP growth of at least 10%. International capital raising is becoming a key part of the equation, but reforms will be needed to attract investors and optimize funding costs.
Massive funding needs stretch the limits of bank lending
In April 2026, the Vietnamese parliament approved a resolution on the five-year socio-economic development plan for 2026-2030, setting a target of average annual GDP growth of at least 10%.
To achieve this goal, total society's investment over the period is projected at around VND38,500 trillion ($1.49 trillion), roughly double the level recorded in the previous five-year period.
This translates into an annual funding requirement of about VND7,700 trillion ($298.05 billion), equivalent to 40% of nominal GDP. Public investment is expected to average around VND1,600 trillion ($61.93 billion) a year, accounting for less than 22% of total capital needs. The remaining 78% will have to come from the private domestic sector, foreign direct investment (FDI) and the financial system, according to estimates by VIS Ratings.
Meanwhile, outstanding bank credit had reached around 146% of GDP by the end of 2025, putting Vietnam among the most highly leveraged banking markets in ASEAN. The World Bank has warned that rapid credit growth is increasing risks to the financial system, stressing the need to maintain prudent lending standards and closely monitor credit quality.
These figures highlight the limits of a growth model that relies primarily on bank financing, particularly as the economy requires long-term capital for transport infrastructure, energy, logistics and large-scale investment projects.
On the stock market, total capital raised through share and bond issuance reached VND731.6 trillion ($28.32 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, up 85.6% from a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Finance. Despite the strong growth, the amount remains modest compared with annual funding needs of around VND7,700 trillion ($298.05 billion).
Dr. Can Van Luc, chief economist at state-controlled bank BIDV, also noted that bank credit currently supplies about 51% of the economy’s total funding and is expected to account for an even larger share. Meanwhile, capital mobilized through the capital markets, including equities, corporate bonds and government bonds, meets only around 23% of funding needs.
Household savings represent another potential source of financing. Before 2026, Vietnam’s savings rate averaged around 35% of GDP, exceeding the actual investment rate of approximately 31% and creating a gap of four percentage points of GDP, according to Luc. However, the savings rate is forecast to decline to around 33% of GDP in 2026, suggesting that the scope for mobilizing domestic resources also warrants a more cautious assessment.
Public debt has headroom, but the investor base must expand
As funding needs rise, Vietnam’s public debt remains below the safety thresholds set by the National Assembly, the country's legislature. Government estimates put public debt at around 35-36% of GDP at the end of 2025, government debt at 33-34% and external debt at 31-32%. Compared with the respective ceilings of around 60%, 50% and 50% of GDP for 2026-2030, these figures indicate that Vietnam still has room to borrow.
Nguyen Quang Thuan, co-founder, chairman and CEO of FiinGroup, said the country's relatively safe public debt levels gave the government scope to consider additional borrowing to support development goals. Funding could be raised in both domestic and international markets.
Domestically, Vietnam has established a foundation for government bond issuance and trading. However, the investor base remains concentrated among banks, insurance companies and Vietnam Social Security, while foreign investors account for only around 0.1% of outstanding local-currency government bonds.
This structure has a positive aspect: it helps sustain relatively stable domestic demand and supports low bond issuance yields. But as Vietnam seeks to expand the market and diversify its investor base, attracting new sources of capital will become increasingly challenging.
Thuan said that with yields on 10-year government bonds recently hovering around 4%, after previously standing at just above 3%, investors might consider alternatives such as bank deposits if they offer more attractive returns. The government therefore needs to strike a balance between accelerating market reforms, broadening the investor base and allowing market forces to play a greater role in order to raise capital efficiently while keeping public debt under control.
In international markets, Vietnam also faces challenges related to its sovereign credit rating, credit conditions and global interest rates. With yields on five-year U.S. Treasury bonds, denominated in U.S. dollars, rising to around 5%, international borrowing costs are also coming under pressure.
Market reforms should not wait for interest rates to fall
Thuan said Vietnam should not delay necessary reforms simply because interest rates remain high. Improving the sovereign credit rating and developing the capital markets should be treated as long-term strategic priorities, rather than measures to be pursued only when immediate funding needs arise.
Maybank Investment Bank (MSVN) said Vietnam could achieve a structural reduction in foreign borrowing costs by securing an investment-grade sovereign credit rating, even as global borrowing costs remain elevated for an extended period. Based on previous rating upgrades, foreign borrowing costs could fall by around 150-250 basis points, it said.
MSVN expects the government to make achieving investment-grade sovereign status a top priority and accelerate the process as early as 2027. One proposed measure is to establish a dedicated sovereign credit rating task force, performing functions similar to those of investor relations (IR) teams at companies. The body would provide credit rating agencies with comprehensive and accurate information on Vietnam’s macroeconomic conditions and development plans.
Such reforms would not only expand the government's funding capacity but also help strengthen the capital markets. The government bond market, in particular, plays a foundational role in establishing a benchmark yield curve and pricing other debt instruments.
Thuan said mutual funds, sovereign wealth funds, international funds and development finance institutions were all interested in whether Vietnam could establish a sufficiently reliable benchmark yield curve. Without a credible reference rate derived from government bonds, companies would find it difficult to determine appropriate funding costs that reflect the risk profiles of their projects when seeking capital in international markets.
Once this foundation is in place, international investors would be better positioned not only to participate in overseas issuances of Vietnamese bonds denominated in foreign currencies, but also to increase their investments in local-currency bonds. "This is also a path taken by some countries in the region. For Vietnam, attracting international investors to the local-currency bond market could diversify demand while reducing reliance on foreign-currency borrowing and the associated risks from exchange-rate fluctuations," the FiinGroup chairman said.
International capital raising needs to be part of a broader strategy to develop domestic capital markets, broaden the investor base and improve creditworthiness. By establishing more channels for raising long-term capital at reasonable costs, Vietnam can ease pressure on its banking system while mobilizing resources for infrastructure projects and new growth drivers.
The challenge is not simply to find additional funding, but to build a financial structure capable of supporting Vietnam’s ambition to achieve double-digit growth in 2026-2030.

articles.title: Indonesia Finance Chief Enlists Business Lobby to Drive 7% Investment Pace as Deficit Outlook Widens - InvestorTrust
articles.summary: Indonesia Finance Chief Enlists Business Lobby to Drive 7% Investment Pace as Deficit Outlook Widens  InvestorTrust
articles.full_text:
Indonesia Finance Chief Enlists Business Lobby to Drive 7% Investment Pace as Deficit Outlook Widens
Key Takeaways
| ● | Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara called on the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry to accelerate direct investment expansion to 7% in 2027 to complement state spending. | 
| ● | The government lifted its 2026 fiscal deficit projection from 2.68% to 2.85% of gross domestic product, or Rp 734 trillion ($46.16 billion), driven by disaster relief and climbing energy subsidy bills. | 
| ● | Sovereign wealth manager BPI Danantara and the state budget are positioned as complementary pillars to crowd in private capital and upgrade grassroots enterprises into global value chains. | 
| ● | Kadin leadership concluded its annual leadership meeting with three core recommendations and an "Indonesia Incorporated" blueprint scheduled for presentation to President Prabowo Subianto. | 
JAKARTA, Investortrust.id — Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara issued a direct appeal to Indonesia’s corporate leadership on Friday, urging the private sector to step forward as the primary driver of capital formation and target a 7% investment expansion in 2027.
Addressing delegates at the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kadin) National Leadership Meeting (Rapimnas) in Jakarta, Suahasil highlighted the arithmetic boundaries of sovereign spending. The central government budget (APBN) directly accounts for only about 15% of Indonesia’s gross domestic product, which is projected to reach Rp 25,000 trillion ($1.57 trillion). The remaining 85% of the economic engine relies on household consumption, private enterprise investment, and international exports.
"Because of that, investment must indeed expand 7% next year," Suahasil told delegates. "You, the members of Kadin Indonesia, hold a vital role in generating this capital expansion, because direct investment is executed by all of you."
The finance chief's call marks an explicit recognition that state expenditure cannot underwrite national growth ambitions on its own. With global borrowing costs hovering near structural highs and domestic budgets absorbing escalating climate and commodity shocks, sovereign spending must serve as an enabler rather than the sole funder of development. Aligning the private sector behind an aggressive 7% investment pace is essential if Southeast Asia’s largest economy is to achieve the administration’s broader multi-year growth targets without blowing past its statutory 3% fiscal deficit boundary.
Fiscal Headroom Strained by Climate and Fuel Bills
The urgency for private-sector capital mobilization comes as fiscal authorities navigate mounting balance-sheet strains. Suahasil disclosed that the government has revised its 2026 state budget design, widening the projected deficit from an initial 2.68% of GDP, or Rp 689 trillion, to 2.85% of GDP, representing Rp 734 trillion ($46.16 billion).
The deficit revision was driven by an expansion in sovereign spending, which increased from Rp 3,843 trillion to Rp 3,942 trillion ($247.92 billion). The higher expenditures were partially matched by an uptick in state revenues, which climbed from an initial baseline of Rp 3,154 trillion to Rp 3,208 trillion ($201.76 billion).
"When expenditures increase, revenue must climb and the deficit is widened, but we ensure our debt financing remains fully credible," Suahasil explained.
Nearly Rp 100 trillion ($6.28 billion) in additional spending stemmed from unforeseen outlays, notably natural disaster relief operations in Sumatra and across various regions that absorbed approximately Rp 60 trillion ($3.77 billion). Concurrently, international commodity volatility forced the treasury to absorb expanded energy subsidies and fuel compensation to keep domestic retail prices steady and protect daily commerce.
To cushion the impact on the treasury, fiscal managers executed internal reallocations of roughly Rp 200 trillion across line-item budgets before absorbing the net Rp 300 trillion total spending increase. Through September 2026, the realized fiscal deficit stood at Rp 319 trillion ($20.06 billion), or 1.24% of GDP, anchored by a positive primary balance surplus of Rp 125.5 trillion ($7.89 billion) and debt interest payments totaling Rp 444.5 trillion ($27.95 billion).
Danantara and the State Budget as Dual Capital Catalysts
To bridge the gap between sovereign fiscal limits and national development needs, Suahasil framed the state budget and newly established sovereign asset agency Badan Pengelola Investasi Daya Anagata Nusantara (Danantara) as synchronized institutional engines.
While the APBN manages public welfare, infrastructure outlays, human capital development, and tax incentives, Danantara is tasked with mobilizing strategic capital and crowding in private participation. Suahasil reiterated that this framework must extend downward to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), which comprise 99% of national business units, generate 60% of GDP, and absorb 97% of the domestic workforce.
"Danantara and the business community—all of you in this room—will translate this foundation into direct investment, physical production, job creation, and sustainable growth," Suahasil told corporate leaders. "This is our collective synergy to advance public welfare and safeguard macroeconomic stability."
Kadin Readies "Indonesia Incorporated" Blueprint for the Palace
The corporate sector signaled ready alignment with the treasury's agenda. Concluding the Rapimnas deliberations on Friday evening, Kadin Chairman Anindya Novyan Bakrie announced that the chamber has codified three core strategic recommendations to bolster the economy against global headwinds: constructing institutional shock absorbers to safeguard corporate cash flow and household purchasing power, guaranteeing domestic industrial raw material supplies through closed-loop ecosystems, and establishing legal certainty to anchor capital.
Kadin Vice Chairman for Investment, Downstreaming, Energy, and Environment Bobby Gafur Umar pushed back against claims that the domestic investment climate is losing traction, pointing out that cumulative direct investment of Rp 1,539.2 trillion ($96.8 billion) through the third quarter of 2026 met statutory benchmarks under the Ministry of Investment. Umar emphasized that strategic capital allocations—ranging from manufacturing facilities and power utilities to industrial downstreaming—are long-term balance-sheet commitments that reflect enduring commercial confidence.
Anindya confirmed that a leadership delegation from the business lobby has secured an audience with President Prabowo Subianto on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026, to formally submit the findings of the national leadership assembly.
The upcoming meeting with the head of state is intended to institutionalize the "Indonesia Incorporated" doctrine, solidifying structured cooperation between state agencies and private operators to buffer the domestic economy while unlocking high-value global trade corridors.

articles.title: Vietnam’s oil and gas sector seeks new growth avenues as easy discoveries fade - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam’s oil and gas sector seeks new growth avenues as easy discoveries fade  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam’s major oil and gas fields are declining, while marginal and remote offshore reserves are increasingly costly to develop. The 2026 Petroleum Law aims to ease regulatory hurdles, but unlocking remaining resources will require advanced technology, timely investment and a broader growth model beyond extraction.
From ageing fields to the challenge of efficient production
Vietnam’s oil and gas industry is at a turning point. Fields that once delivered substantial output after decades of production are gradually declining, while future growth increasingly depends on developing smaller and marginal fields and applying technology to recover additional resources. This is not merely a technical challenge but also a test of investment mechanisms and the industry's ability to execute projects effectively.
Speaking at the forum "Developing Vietnam’s oil and gas Industry: Ensuring sustainable growth" on Thursday, Dao Quang Binh, vice chairman of the Vietnam Economic Science Association, underscored the importance of energy in general and the oil and gas industry in particular to national energy security and macroeconomic stability.
However, he said the sector was facing mounting pressure from the natural decline of major fields, global geopolitical volatility and Vietnam’s commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050.
These challenges mean the industry's development strategy can no longer focus solely on maintaining output from existing fields. At the forum, Vu Quang Minh, former Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs, noted that many fields were approaching the end of their production life.
The remaining opportunities were largely concentrated in marginal and remote fields that are difficult to develop and may be located in geopolitically sensitive areas. Vietnam's oil and gas production has fallen to around half its 2004 peak, Minh noted, adding that the Bach Ho field had been in production for 40 years.
This highlights the distinction between remaining resources and commercially viable production opportunities. Smaller and marginal fields may still contain substantial reserves, but project scale, geological conditions, distance from existing infrastructure and investment costs present significant obstacles to economic viability. Without sufficiently flexible mechanisms to allocate risks and incentivize investors, remaining resources may prove difficult to convert into commercial production.
Pham Truong Giang, deputy director of the Center for Petroleum Exploration and Production Research at the Vietnam Petroleum Institute, also pointed out that small and marginal field projects offered considerable potential in terms of in-place reserves but faced the greatest risks related to investment costs and economic returns. Removing policy and regulatory barriers is therefore essential to bringing these projects into development, he said.
Another avenue for growth lies in improving recovery rates at existing fields. Giang said the average recovery factor at producing oil and gas fields worldwide was only around 30%, meaning a substantial proportion of underground resources remained unrecovered. This represents an opportunity to deploy new technologies, optimize operations and improve production efficiency. Petrovietnam, the Vietnam National Industry-Energy Group, and its subsidiaries have stepped up research, evaluation and the application of enhanced oil recovery solutions, he said.
The industry's challenge, therefore, is not simply to discover new fields but also to extract more value from existing assets while making technically challenging projects economically viable. Against this backdrop, the 2026 Petroleum Law is expected to establish a more suitable legal framework for the industry's changing operating conditions.
New law opens opportunities, but growth cannot rely on extraction alone
One of the key features of the 2026 Petroleum Law is an incentive framework tailored to the level of difficulty faced by individual projects, including specific provisions for marginal fields. According to Phan Duc Hieu, a member of the National Assembly's Economic and Financial Committee, marginal fields may qualify for a corporate income tax rate of 25%, an export tax rate of 5% and a full cost-recovery mechanism. The law also aims to simplify administrative procedures, clarify the allocation of authority and give businesses greater operational autonomy.
These changes could have significant practical implications for projects in which high investment costs have made profitability uncertain. More appropriate cost-recovery arrangements and incentives would give investors a stronger basis for assessing returns and considering the development of fields that were previously commercially unattractive. However, incentives alone will not guarantee project implementation. Their effectiveness will also depend on the quality of project assessments, production technologies and execution capabilities.
Dang Thu Hoai, head of the sectoral and local economic research department at the Institute for Policy and Strategy Studies, emphasized the strategic importance of oil and gas and the broader energy sector to economic growth, technological self-reliance and national autonomy. Oil and gas are not merely inputs for numerous economic sectors but are also closely linked to energy security, the maritime economy and the need to shift towards a higher-quality, greener and more self-reliant growth model, she said.
From this perspective, the industry's ambitions must extend beyond extracting additional resources. The new law also encourages research, development, testing, application and technology transfer to expand high-tech petroleum engineering services, particularly products and services capable of replacing imports or competing in international markets. This provides a foundation for the industry to gradually expand its capabilities beyond extraction into higher value-added industrial activities and services.
Nevertheless, the new framework may fall short of its potential if investment decisions and project implementation conditions continue to face delays. Nguyen Hung Dung, vice chairman of the Vietnam Petroleum Association, said appropriate pricing mechanisms were essential to ensuring projects could move forward. If investors continued to wait for decisions on pricing and power purchase agreements, project timelines would remain under pressure, he said.
Dung also highlighted the need to clarify PetroVietnam's roles, given that the group acts as the host country's representative, an investor and, potentially, a contractor in the same projects. Greater autonomy must be accompanied by clear decision-making and a willingness to act, he said. Otherwise, projects could face prolonged delays, with economic returns deteriorating over time.
This bottleneck needs to be addressed alongside legislative reforms. The law may grant businesses greater autonomy and establish more favorable mechanisms, but the ultimate outcome will depend on how responsibilities are allocated, how stakeholders coordinate and how quickly decisions are translated into action. For marginal fields in particular, where project economics are highly sensitive to costs and timing, delays could erode the very advantages that the new incentives are designed to create.
In the longer term, the industry's development strategy must also move beyond resource extraction. Dang Thanh Tung, deputy head of Petrovietnam's strategy department, said the country's resource potential was no longer as abundant as in the past, requiring the group to transform its development model around three pillars: energy, industry and high-quality technical services.
According to the direction outlined at the forum, the industry needs to develop the gas value chain, expand downstream refining and petrochemical processing, strengthen mechanical engineering and manufacturing capabilities, and enhance offshore technical services. Digital technologies and data applications will also be important in optimizing operations and improving recovery rates.
The industry's accumulated technical expertise could also provide a foundation for expansion into new sectors. Former Deputy Foreign Minister Vu Quang Minh cited PetroVietnam Technical Services Corporation (PTSC) as an example, pointing to its fabrication and export of offshore wind turbine foundations and substations for international markets. These projects demonstrate how capabilities developed through the oil and gas industry can be converted into industrial expertise serving other energy sectors.
The end of the era of easy oil and gas discoveries does not mean Vietnam's petroleum industry has run out of growth opportunities. The challenge lies in turning technically difficult resources into economically viable production while transforming accumulated expertise and engineering capabilities into higher-value industrial and service activities.
The new Petroleum Law could open the door to the next investment cycle. Whether the industry can capitalize on that opportunity will depend on the pace of policy implementation, technological capabilities and its determination to shift from resource extraction towards broader industrial development.

articles.summary: National Assembly representatives from the province proposed solutions to improve the quality of growth and leverage the internal strengths of the economy.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On the afternoon of October 30th, continuing the program of the Second Session, the National Assembly discussed in the plenary hall the situation regarding the implementation of the socio-economic development plan for 2026 and the projected plan for 2027; the situation regarding the implementation of the state budget in 2026, the budget estimate and allocation plan for the central budget in 2027; the situation regarding the implementation of the public investment plan in 2026 and the projected public investment plan for 2027; the final accounts of the state budget for 2025; the summary of the implementation of Resolution No. 66/2013/QH13 of the National Assembly and the completion of the investment and construction of the Ho Chi Minh Highway project with a scale of two lanes.
During the discussion, National Assembly delegates from Ninh Binh province proposed numerous solutions to improve the quality of growth, ensure macroeconomic stability, and enhance the capabilities of domestic businesses.
Growth must be linked to macroeconomic stability and improving the people's living standards.
Speaking in the assembly hall, delegate Tran Thi Hong Thanh, Provincial Party Committee member and Deputy Head of the Ninh Binh Provincial Delegation of National Assembly Deputies, stated that alongside the positive and comprehensive results in all fields, the requirement is that the economy needs to grow at a higher rate but must be based on a solid foundation; more resources must be mobilized but must be transformed into productivity, jobs, and real income.
Delegates proposed that the Government focus on five key solutions. First, managing growth based on realistic scenarios and maintaining macroeconomic stability. GDP growth in the first nine months was 9.01%, but to achieve 10% or more for the whole year, growth in the fourth quarter must reach approximately 12.5%, while 27 out of 34 localities have not yet met their targets. Therefore, it is necessary to quantify the contribution of each sector and locality; develop growth and inflation scenarios corresponding to fluctuations in energy prices, interest rates, and international trade; and clearly identify risk thresholds and response plans. Delegates also noted that the CPI in the first nine months increased by 4.52%, while real purchasing power only increased by nearly 8%. Therefore, price management should follow a carefully planned roadmap, ensuring the supply of essential goods, strictly dealing with speculation and price manipulation, and providing support to those affected, especially low-income earners and workers.
Secondly, the focus should shift from capital mobilization to efficient capital allocation, ensuring financial safety. According to the delegates, credit increased by 11.7%, higher than the 10.7% increase in capital mobilization, while the credit-to-GDP ratio is already high. The delegates proposed that the Government closely monitor liquidity, maturity mismatches, bad debts, and credit concentration; and periodically publicize risk indicators to enable early intervention. Credit expansion should be linked to repayment capacity and project efficiency, while strictly controlling interconnected risks between banks, bonds, and real estate. In the long term, bank credit cannot continue to bear the majority of medium- and long-term capital needs. Focus should be placed on developing a transparent corporate bond market, improving the quality of information disclosure and credit ratings, encouraging long-term investors, and strictly addressing violations to strengthen confidence.
Thirdly, improve the efficiency of public investment and remove bottlenecks in energy infrastructure. Each project needs to be reviewed, clearly identifying obstacles, responsibilities, and completion feasibility; capital should be reallocated from slow-moving projects or those lacking the necessary conditions to projects with high absorption capacity and efficiency. For transportation, electricity, and energy projects, there needs to be synchronized coordination between planning, land acquisition, material sources, transmission grids, financing arrangements, and power purchase agreements. Simultaneously, the energy reserve strategy should be finalized soon, and contingency plans for electricity and fuel sources should be developed based on adverse scenarios.

Fourth, enhance the endogenous capacity of the economy, especially Vietnamese enterprises, science and technology, and labor productivity. This includes policies to attract FDI linked to commitments and measurable results regarding technology transfer, human resource training, the use of Vietnamese suppliers, and the increase of domestic added value. Simultaneously, directly address difficulties related to capital, land, standards, and markets for small and medium-sized enterprises, supporting industries, and domestic suppliers.
Fifth, ensure that reforms reach the grassroots level and that people benefit from the fruits of growth. Delegates emphasized that decentralization and delegation of power are only effective when authority is accompanied by human resources, funding, data, and accountability; timely support is needed for localities lacking specialized personnel, overloaded with paperwork, or lacking infrastructure.
To put the above solutions into practice, delegate Tran Thi Hong Thanh proposed that the Government create a list of key tasks for 2027, clearly identifying the lead agency, deadline, resources, outputs, and evaluation indicators. Tasks that are behind schedule must clearly state the causes, responsibilities, and remedial measures; resources should be prioritized for areas capable of producing tangible results.
Enhancing the capacity of Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in supply chains.
Agreeing with the draft law, delegate Pham Hung Thang, Provincial Party Committee member and Deputy Head of the Ninh Binh Provincial Delegation of National Assembly Deputies, suggested that the Government pay attention to improving the capacity of Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in supply chains, creating and retaining more value for the national economy.
According to the delegates, Politburo Resolutions No. 68, 57, and No. 10 have set requirements for enhancing the capacity of domestic enterprises, strengthening linkages, and promoting technology transfer. The important thing is to concretize these policies into measurable results, including an increase in the number of Vietnamese enterprises becoming suppliers and participating in value chains; and a greater amount of added value being created and retained domestically. The evaluation of investment attraction effectiveness needs to shift from the number of projects and capital scale to the quality of linkages and the ripple effect on Vietnamese enterprises.
Analyzing import and export data for the first nine months of 2026, delegates noted that exports increased by 24.5%, while imports increased by 36.7%. Domestic businesses experienced a large trade deficit, while foreign-invested businesses had a trade surplus. This highlights the need to improve production capacity, product quality, and the ability of domestic businesses to participate in value chains.
Delegates pointed out that the current bottleneck is that many businesses have not yet met the requirements of upstream businesses in terms of technology, management, quality standards, traceability, and stable delivery capabilities. Therefore, the effectiveness of support should be evaluated by whether businesses become suppliers, secure stable contracts, and increase added value. The presence of large economic groups cannot be equated with the effectiveness of technology transfer if domestic businesses still mainly engage in simple processing, relying on external sources for design, materials, components, and advanced techniques.

The delegates also stated that the Prime Minister has issued decisions approving the Program for the Development of Supporting Industries for the period 2026-2035; and approving the Project to promote Vietnamese enterprises' direct participation in foreign distribution networks by 2030. Along with these development programs and projects, at this session, the National Assembly is discussing, considering, and is expected to approve many projects, including the Law amending and supplementing several articles of the Investment Law and the Law on Supporting the Development of Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises, with many new regulations on supporting the enhancement of domestic enterprise capacity, supporting supply chain development, and participation in supply chain value chains. The next important step is to quickly concretize and connect policies with practical needs and organize their unified and effective implementation.
Support should begin with the purchasing needs, technical standards, and supplier selection criteria of leading enterprises, including foreign-invested enterprises. Based on an assessment of Vietnamese enterprises' capabilities, the State should provide support in areas that are lacking or weak, such as testing, quality certification, process improvement, technical training, and equipment modernization. The State's role is to connect and support domestic enterprises in reducing costs to participate in the supply chain; purchasing decisions remain with the enterprises, ensuring fair competition and compliance with international commitments.
